Mr. Speaker, I desire, with your permission, on behalf of the Canadian Battlefields Memorials Commission to advise members of this House that the first stage of the competition in design for the eight battlefield memorials to be erected in France and Belgium by the Canadian Government was concluded on the 15th instant. By that date one hundred and sixty sets of designs had been received. These were judged anonymously by the following Board of Assessors: Professor C. H. Reilly, Liverpool, nominated by the Royal Institute of British Architects; Professor Paul P. Cret, nominated by the Societies des Architects Paris, and Professor Frank Darling, nominated by the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada. Of these one hundred and sixty competitors, seventeen designers were selected to enter the final stage of the competition. This will involve the submission of models of their designs. The conditions for the final stage of the competition are now being prepared and will be sent to the seventeen selected designers in the course of a few days.
The successful competitors of the first stage have been notified officially and an article also appeared in yesterday's papers giving their names and addresses. PRIME MINISTERS' CONFERENCE On the Orders of the Day:

Mr. Speaker, yesterday afternoon the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) made

a statement to the House with reference to the approaching: Prime Ministers' Conference to be held in London in June next, and in course of his observations he said that:
-the June meeting would he of a special and preliminary character having in view the necessity of discussing-
And then he proceeded to enumerate a series of subjects. Within a few hours of that statement being made in this House, Mr. Winston Churchill is reported to have made a speech in London, and in dealing with the subject of the conference he is alleged to have said:
The Conference was not to he a temporary or occasional affair or a periodical institution, hut a meeting of the regular Imperial Cabinet. He thought they could anticipate a properly successful series of discussions.
I desire to ask the right hon. gentleman if he can explain the difference of opinion that evidently exists with regard to the character and scope of the approaching conference, and whether his definition or that of Mr. Winston Churchill is the correct one?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the definition that I gave in the outline not Only of the character but of the proposed proceedings was based upon communications that had passed between the Government of Great Britain and ourselves, and the references to it that appeared more noticeably at the end of the statement were based more exclusively upon the view of Canada. As to whether it should be described as an Imperial Cabinet or as Prime Ministers' Conference, I think the latter nomenclature is the better. The Imperial War Cabinet is the only Imperial Cabinet that has ever met, and it met for purposes that had to do with the temporary condition of war. This is the first meeting of Prime Ministers of this character. Whether it becomes permanent or not, it is too soon yet to predict.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to draw the attention of the Prime Minister to a matter of urgent public importance in view of the fact that the income tax returns and payments must be made this week. On March 29 the attention of the Government was drawn to the difficulty experienced by the public in being compelled to compute the tax, and the uneasiness in the public mind with regard to certain penalties which might be applied. The suggestion was made then-I think it was by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux)-that the method of last year should be continued this year, by which the statement was made out by the tax' payer, a bill forwarded to the taxpayer by the department, and the amount then paid in due course. The Prime Minister at that time replied as follows:
The Minister of Finance is unfortunately absent, being engaged this afternoon addressing an audience in the city. However, I feel safe in intimating-though nothing in the nature of a definite announcement can 'b'e made until his return-that the regulations have been under reconsideration, and I believe that the Minister of Finance has a method which he thinks of proposing that would not be open to objections of the nature suggested by the hon. member. I will call his attention to the matter.
So far as I know, Mr. Speaker, no further announcement has been made with regard to that, although the matter is of very considerable importance. In view of the uneasiness in the public mind and of the undoubted difficulty and perhaps inability on the part of taxpayers not only to make

out their statements but to compute the amount of tax which they have to pay, I would ask the Government whether they are ready to announce any new method, and if so what the nature of it is?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Before the committee enters upon a detailed discussion of the Estimates of the department I should like to make a general statement regarding some of the features of our immigration policy and regarding immigration matters generally. I think it will probably save time and be very helpful to' the members in the detailed discussion which will follow.

It will be remembered that some time ago the member for St. Mary's division of Montreal (Mr. Desiauriers) introduced a resolution, the object of which was to provide for the total exclusion of all immigrants during what he considered to be the abnormal period through which we are passing. At that time we had a very considerable discussion, many members taking part in the debate. It will be recalled that it occurred on a Wednesday afternoon; the House was not sitting that night, and the debate was concluded at six o'clock upon my suggestion that the hon. gentleman should withdraw his motion, that an opportunity would be given later in the session for a full discussion. I trust that at this time I shall not be transgressing the rules if I make some reference to the debate that occurred then. On that occasion a number of questions were asked and some criticisms were made against certain features of the work being carried on by the Department of Immigration. At the outset I would like to place before the committee very squarely the main question of policy that was raised in that debate. It was this: Should we at this time absolutely close the door against all immigration? It was asserted that every person of sound mind and sound body who was willing to work should be admitted to Canada, regardless of all other considerations. On the other hand, there were those who held that we should take into consideration economic, social and other conditions existing in Canada and that the numbers admitted should be limited. That was the main question in that discussion, and in order that the committee may understand what were the views taken by members on that occasion I would like to make some very brief references to what was then said by several hon. gentlemen.
The member for St. Mary, who introduced the resolution, took the ground that there should be absolute exclusion; that no immigrants should be admitted at the present time. The hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx) who followed and who seconded the motion, agreed in very large measure with the view taken by the member for St. Mary. He stated, however, that he would admit farmers but that there was no necessity for admitting artisans, labourers or others of that class. The member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) who followed, stated very clearly and very distinctly that in his judgment, while Canada needed men for the land, we should not admit any artisans at all; that there were sufficient artisans and

labourers in Canada at present to take care of all the work that was being offered. The member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) favoured rather the open door, as he said, with modifications. He was, however, a litle careful not to indicate exactly the nature of the modifications that he would consider wise. He intimated as well -not very definitely, but you can read it into his speech-that Canada at this time should be a land of refuge for the war-weary and the heavy laden of Europe. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Boyce) took the ground that every honest man who was willing to work should be allowed to enter Canada, no matter where he came from, no matter what his nationality was, no matter what his views were, no matter whether he was assimilable in Canada or not -regardless of any or all conditions. The hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) stated that, in his judgment, there were at the present time a sufficient number of artisans in Canada, and that we should bar the further entry of people of that class. He was very much opposed to the present money qualifications. The hon. member for New Wesminister (Mr. McQuarrie), stated that he had in the country many men who were not able to secure work, and that we should not admit others while these conditions existed. He took the ground that there should be the strictest kind of supervision as regards admitting immigrants to Canada at the present time. The hon. member for Stratheona (Mr. Douglas) took the ground that the regulations to-day were too restrictive, that they were shutting out too many people, and he gave us an instance of certain cases of settlements in western Canada where the people had got along very well. He evidently had in mind some people who had been shut out under the existing law, and he took the ground that those restrictions should be removed. The hon. member for Oxford South (Mr. Sutherland) stated that we should be most careful as to the class of immigrants that we admitted. He intimated that they should be in sympathy with our laws and institutions, and that any people in any part of the world who were not in sympathy with our laws and institutions should be debarred entry to Canada. The hon. member for Glengarry and Stormont (Mr. Kennedy) expressed surprise that anyone would advocate the barring out of suitable immigrants. The hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Baldwin) took the ground that we should have a system under which anyone can come to Canada who is law abiding and willing to work. The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Wilson) agreed that there should be restrictions as regards certain classes. He said that what we need most of all is people for the land, and he took the ground that the present money qualification, which requires each male adult immigrant to have $250 in cash, should be removed, because it is likely to operate to prevent desirable people from coming to Canada. I need not quote any further.
It will be noticed that in that discussion two distinct views were expressed, one favouring the open door and the other the closed door. Then there was a middle view advocated by hon. members who expressed the idea that we should select and allow people to come to Canada, very great care being exercised as to the classes we admitted.
During the course of recent weeks, the press of Canada has contained a good many editorials and articles on this question of immigration, and merely for the purpose of getting the general question well before the committee, I desire to quote a few extracts from some of the leading Canadian papers. These are nearly typical, because there is in Canada scarcely a paper that has not had a good deal to say on this subject during the course of the past few months. The first quotation, which is very brief, is from the Manitoba Free Press, of Winnipeg. Under date of March 22, 1921, the Manitoba Free Press stated:
For some years past the Free Press has declared over and over again with all but damnable iteration that the true national policy of Canada at this stage is to develop our natural resources and primarily to get people on the land and keep them there.
The Toronto iStar on the same date stated:
The country is not in need of a further influx of city dwellers.
Then it goes on to express the same idea as the Manitoba Free Press, that is, that we should admit people freely for going on the land.
The Montreal Gazette on the following day, March 23,-1921, stated:
While farm labourers and domestic servants are more favoured, the financial bars have been raised against both skilled and unskilled labour. Temporary unemployment is not a valid reason for permanent adherence to a policy which holds the Canadian industrial field as a preserve for the labour now i.n it to the detriment of industry which cannot in such conditions expand except at increased labour cost.
In other words, the Gazette favoured the open door. It would admit artisans of all

classes freely, simply on the ground that we should not set up conditions which would establish in Canada a preserve, as it states, for existing labour in this country. The Mail and Empire, on March 22, in an editorial, stated:
Everything in reason should be done to encourage the right kind of people to cast their lot in Canada and enlist in the work of making this the great nation it ought to be, and at the same time every precaution should be taken to prevent Canada from being used as a dumping ground for the ofif-scourings of other populations.
.The Calgary Herald, on May 28, stated- this view is held by a good many people throughout Canada and by many hon. members in this House:
Immigration activities can safely be restricted for some years to the British Isles, the United States and the northern countries of Europe. Swedes, Norwegians, Danes and Icelanders have been amongst our best settlers. These fields will offer ample scope for the work of our immigration agencies for many years to come.
Those editorials all appeared somewhere about March 22 to 26, and I am sure they were based on two utterances made by prominent gentlemen in the country, the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), leader of the Agrarian group, and Mr. Beatty. 1 desire to quote these as well. I hope I am not wearying the House in doing so, because I am endeavouring to lay a basis for a discussion which we shall doubtless have on the general question of policy.
Did the hon. gentleman quote any eastern papers?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes. The Toronto Star and the Montreal Gazette. I find that the hon. member for Marquette, addressing a gathering in Toronto, made this statement as representing his view:
The Government should inaugurate a vigorous immigration policy bringing into Canada only people suitable for agricultural work and assimilable withj our population, adaptable for future citizenship through the possession of its potentialities. Those should be settled along our national railways and furnish the nucleus for future profit-paying traffic.
This is another quotation from the hon. member for Marquette, and from a speech which he delivered in Toronto. It appears in the Manitoba Free Press, of Winnipeg:
I am convinced that the only manner in which we can escape from the difficulties that lie ahead is by an increase in the population of this country. And that must come, largely, through immigration. Now, when we get immigration to this country we want to use some discrimination in whom we are taking to Canada. Our possibilities are such, our great fertile plains and all parts of Canada are such, that we can bring people to Canada, induce people to come

to Canada, and, if necessary, we should be able to assist them a little bit after they come here. This policy of immigration should go hand in hand with the railway problem. We want to bring people to this land, and, I submit, they should be people who will go on the farms.
We have enough people In our cities. I am told you have what is called a bread-line in the city of Toronto. Well, I want to tell you they have no bread-lines out in the rural districts of Canada, and, consequently, we do not wish to congregate more people in our cities. We wish to bring to Canada people who will go on the land, and cultivate the land, and produce off the land. We can get them. There are (ots of them available who will come here, attracted by our cheap lands, and we want to give all the assistance possible, and we want to settle these people along the lines of the national railways and create potential business for the roads.
That was the view then expressed by the hon. member for Marquette on the general question of policy. As I have said, a public statement was also made by Mr. Beatty, president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, which was very freely discussed in the editorial and news columns of the press throughout Canada. I dare say most hon. members have read that statement, but I think it will do no harm at this juncture to read it again:
I am afraid that many people in Canada do not sufficiently realize that the most urgent and essential need to-day is increase in population, not only to provide traffic for the railways, but also to help pay our enormous national indebtedness. So far as the railways are concerned, the national railways are even more concerned in this demand for population than the Canadian Pacific, owing to the extent of sparsely populate^ country in which so much of their mileage is located. It was an aggressive immigration propaganda that built up the Canadian Pacific, and without immigration the prespects of the Canadian National are, in my opinion, hopeless.
Any legislation which would stem the tide of desirable immigration must inevitably pile up further deficits, for immigration is Canada's great salvation. Mr. Crerar, who was speaking particularly in the interests of the national railways, struck the right note when he declared before the Canadian Club in Montreal, that a wise and vigorous immigration policy would help solve the problem. Mr. Crerar also referred in another address to the foreign born immigrants, commending the progress they had made in Western Canada and pointing out that over fifty per cent of the students at Manitoba University were of foreign parentage.
The same evidence is contributed in an interesting article in the "Grain Growers' Guide," in reference to the three hundred thousand Ukrainians in Western Canada, in which it is stated that these people of sturdy farming stock from Central Europe have four large educational institutes at Saskatoon, Winnipeg and Edmonton, respectively, and had become a real asset to Canada. The people from the Scandinavian countries have made admirable settlers. During the year 1920, nearly 1,600 of these came as immigrants to Canada, of whom only 10 were deported. All of them are thrifty, hard working' people.

I quite agree with those who object to the immigration of city-bred Continentals of poor physique and doubtful health, who would at once drift into slums, or of large communities of foreign born who frankly declare they do not Intend to assimilate with English-speaking Canadians, but I consider it absolutely necessary to the immediate betterment of Canadian financial, commercial and traffic conditions, that the gates of Canada be once more opened not only to the British, French and American immigrant, but also to the Scandinavian and the more desirable type of Continental.
It is not only farm hands and domestics who are required. What progress can Canadian industry make if the skilled mechanic is to be practically shut out? And without Canadian industry where are we to find exports for the Canadian Merchant Marine? We neither can, nor dare stop this tide of desirable immigration, or say to it like Canute, "Thus Far and No Farther."
There is one other question I desire to make. It is taken from an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press, and comments on some of the views expressed in that statement by Mr. Beatty. The Free Press says:
Upon the general need of immigration there is no disagreement; but there is not uniformity of view as to the limitations that, in the general interests of the country, it is desirable to impose. Upon immigrants capable and willing to work on farms, and in the mines and forests, there need be no limitations whatever, as long as they come from the British Isles, or from northern Europe. With respect to immigration from eastern or central Europe, the bars need not be kept up absolutely, but it is obvious that, in view of the problem of assimilating and Cana-dianizing the Slavic elements in our population which is now a subject of concern in all the western provinces, there must be discretion shown, both with respect to the number and the character of immigrants of this class to whom the gates are opened. City-bred immigrants looking for occupation in our cities we do not want; but mere residence or even up-bringing i-n a city does not necessarily unfit a man for country life in Canada.
It is now a little over two years since our Immigation Act was revised and consolidated. At tbat time, as members of the House will recall, we had a very full discussion of the general policy involved. The point was raised then as to whether or not our law should be made .rigid, that is to say, whether in the law itself there should be set out in detail the classes of people that we should admit to Canada. We had a very full discussion of the subject, part of the discussion arising out of a resolution introduced by the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn). It will be remembered that he proposed at that time that we should clearly set out in the law the peoples of Europe and Asia that we would not admit to Canada. That view finally did not prevail. The House came to the conclusion that our law should be left in a more lax state that is, that
discretionary power should be placed in the hands of the Government and the minister in charge of the administration of the law. We were given power to make regulations limiting the numbers that might come from certain countries, and excluding those who might seek to come from other countires, or to set up bars and restrictions that might have that effect. I merely mention that to indicate the view of the House at that time. Since then we have been operating under that law, and I scarcely need assure hon. members

because there are very few of them who have not had occasion in the past three years to come to me in connection with some immigration question- that a law of that kind is by no means easy to administer. Where you place in the hands of a department or a minister discretionary power, and where you have so many cases of people desiring to come to Canada that are border cases, where judgment must be exercised as to whether^ or not the party in question should be admitted-well, it is not an easy law to administer. I have no doubt that there is every likelihood that mistakes have been made, but where you have a law administered by a fairly large number of officers, a law that depends for its successful administration upon their exercising proper judgment, I am sure every hon. member will realize that cases will arise where, if they themselves had the deciding to do, probably the decision would have been the other way. Consequently there is a feeling that, in so far as a certain number of cases are concerned, some hardship may have resulted; but I can assure the House that, so far as I have come in contact with them, the officials of the department fully realize their duties and responsibilities in that regard and have exercised every reasonable precaution to see that the law is fairly and properly administered.
During recent months particularly there has been a good deal published in the press and a good deal said from the platform in favour of the adoption of a vig' orous immigration policy. These words have been frequently used both outside and in this House, and I am inclined some times to think that those who talk freely of "a vigorous immigration policy" use the expression rather vaguely. I have watched the press of Canada myself very closely, and it js very seldom that I can get anything in the way of an actual, concrete, definite and practical proposal from those who use indefinite language of that kind.
RiEVISED EDITION.

It is all very well simply to say that we must have a real vigorous, progressive immigration policy, but what do you mean by that? What do you intend to do? What is there that should be done that is not done at the present time? I do hope that during the discussion which we shall have here, if we have a discussion, hon. gentlemen who may be inclined to talk along that line will help me by suggesting something quite definite and concrete, something practical, which I shall be able to consider with a view to its adoption if it is both possible and practicable. I think that one of the reasons for the fact that concrete proposals are not made is that very few people have a real knowledge of what is being done by the department, and fewer still a knowledge of what can be done; nor have they much knowledge of what the probable expenditure would be in case certain proposals were carried out. Now, as to the necessity of getting people. I do not see how there can be two opinions on that point. In my view, the policy of total exclusion of immigrants from Canada, in the first place, is impracticable-because it cannot be done; and, in the second place, it would be suicidal to the interests of Canada as a whole if we attempted such a policy. My own view is that we should endeavour to get people just as rapidly as we possibly can, and the reasons for that view have been set out in these articles from which I have quoted. In the first place, so long as we have in Canada millions of acres of the finest land in the world awaiting development, and so long as there are thousands of people outside Canada capable of cultivating that land, then on purely humanitarian grounds, if upon no other, we should not put up any unreasonable bar to prevent those pepole from coming to our country. In the second place, as we all know, provincial and federal governments in Canada, during the course of the last twenty or thirty years, have by various means provided for the building of an enormous railway mileage in this country, far in excess of our actual requirements, and the result to-day is the people have to pay very heavy freight rates and taxation. Now, in my judgment, there is only one real solution for that problem, and that is traffic. These roads must get traffic and get it on a large scale or they will never pay. And you can get traffic only by bringing in people and having them produce, not only on the land, but in our mines, our forests, our fisheries, and in connection with all the other resources we have in this country. So that on that 
ground also, we need people in large numbers and just as quickly as we can possibly get them, and I doubt whether there is a member who does not agree with that proposition. There is a third reason advanced with which I have not so much sympathy, and that is, that we should bring in people in order to decrease our own taxation-I am referring particularly to the national debt growing out of the war. Now, I doubt very much the wisdom of that proposal. While it is true that we have a large debt, it is much smaller than in the case of most other nations that took part in the war, and I am inclined to think that even if we never got people we should be able to take care of that debt. Nevertheless, we should welcome people who could come and help us in that respect. It is a factor that should not be lost sight of in the adoption of any immigration policy. But I do not like the idea of inviting people to come in to take care of our debt, I do not think we should hold out any such invitation; the discharge of our debt should be regarded as incidental in this connection.

You do not want to
put it on the invitation card.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Exactly. Now, granted that we do need people,-and I think we all agree to that,-how are we to get them? I can tell you one very simple way: all we have to do is to take down the restrictions that we have at the present time. We can get thousands upon thousands of people into this country to-day, if we want them, by taking down the bars. The real problem, in my judgment, is not simply to get people; we must get the right kind of people. And in another sense, the real [DOT] problem, or at least one important phase of it, which the department has to deal with at the present time, is not to get people, but to shut out certain classes of people from Canada. I shall deal with some aspects of that question a little later on. I say again that if Canada merely wants people, people standing on two feet with no other qualifications, and if you do not want to consider anything else at all, we shall have not the slightest trouble in getting them. They will come by hundreds of thousands. Is Canada ready for that? Does Canada need certain classes of people at the present time? Would it be detrimental to this country to-day if certain people were allowed in? That is the question to be considered. Those who advocate the adoption of a vigorous immigration policy probably have in mind

that all we need is people. Well, we need something more than that, in my judgment. As every member of the House knows, we have been, and are now still, passing through more or less abnormal times. We have had a serious unemployment situation in Canada, and we are not yet out of the woods. I think the situation is easing off and that there is less unemployment today than there was some time ago; and, as the summer months come along, unemployment, I believe, will be still less. But let me ask this question: So long as the federal Government and the provinces and municipalities, who during all these months have been paying money out to take care of unemployment in our cities, are still faced with the problem, do you think that it would be a wise policy to take down the bars and allow labour, both skilled and unskilled, to flock into this country now? Do you think we should pump in more workers to aggravate that situation? I do not think we should, and that is a fact that must be taken into consideration.
During the last three years, as a matter of fact, the department has right along encouraged mainly three classes of people to come to Canada: the farmer, the agricultural worker, and the household worker or domestic servant. Our energies have been very largely devoted along these lines. Why? Simply on account of the conditions that have prevailed in this country during those three years; on account of the unemployment situation that has existed and still exists in Canada. Have we got back to normal conditions such as existed a few years ago? Take back in 1911, 1912, and 1913, when business of all kinds was booming in this country. I know that out in Western Canada every one of our municipalities was carrying on huge municipal works; construction works were going on everywhere. We never had such a real development, I think, as at that time; we could absorb all sorts of artisans and labour of all classes who came to Canada at that time very freely. Well, if conditions of that kind can be brought about again we will have no difficulty in getting the workers who are necessary to carry on that work. But I maintain that so long as these abnormal conditions existed, this department of the Government has pursued the right policy in holding a check upon certain classes of people who are endeavouring to come to Canada. Now, by that I do not paean that we have entirely excluded skilled or unskilled labour-not at all. As a matter of
163J
fact we have admitted some thousands of these people during the past few years. Whenever we have found that labour of any class either skilled or unskilled is required in Canada, and is not available here, we have not hesitated to get that labour. We have worked in the very closest way with the Labour Department; the two departments have worked hand in hand. Wherever a shortage of labour, either skilled or unskilled, has existed we have not hesitated at all to set our agencies at work to secure whatever labour was required.
Just a word or two, Mr. Chairman, as to the movement of immigration to Canada. I find that a good deal of ignorance exists as to what has been actually taking place this last two or three years. There are a good many people who think nothing has been done, that no people are coming to Canada, that the moneys appropriated by this Parliament from year to year have been wasted, that we might as well stop this expenditure; and reference has been made in a previous debate to the wonderful results secured during the period from 1896 down to 1911 when the West was filled up and all our Prairie Provinces got a very great influx of people. Well, now, <I would be the last man in the world to attempt to detract in any way from the real, national work that was done during that period-it was a great work and deserving of every credit. But our people, as a rule, have no idea as to what has actually taken place, in so far as immigration numbers are concerned, during the past few years, and it is for that reason 1 went through our statistics, and I wish to place some of them before the House in order that hon. gentlemen may realize the facts. I am not going to read all the figures, but I am going to give the totals and averages. Those who live in the West will remember the conditions that existed there prior to 1896 in so far as settlement is concerned. Prom 1897 down to 1901, a five-year period, there were 171,203 people entered all of Canada-171,203 people in a period of five years. Those are statistics, those are facts, those are the records of the department. In other words, during that period of five years from 1897 down to 1901 there was an average each year of only 34,240 people entered Canada. Let us take the next five-year period-but let me pause here just for a moment to make a comparison because I think I had better do that as I go along. During the last few years we had an average immigration into

this country of 133,402. In 1919 there were 117,336 people entered Canada.
Will the minister say if those are the net figures, or is he deducting-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am speaking of the people who entered Canada as immigrants.

Has the minister the
number of who left Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No. I cannot give those figures. There were 117,336 persons entered Canada in 1919-20. For the eleven months of this past year there were 137,468, and it is estimated that when we have - all the figures and they are
4 p.m. finally revised, our immigration for the year will be found to amount to in the neighbourhood of 149,468. This makes a total for these two years of 266,804 people, or an average for the two years of 133,402.
Does that provide for the deportations during the year? I see a list here of something like 13,000 that were deported?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There were no 13,000
deported. They may be rejections, which are very different; I will come to those shortly.

Do the minister's figures
for 1919 include the Hutterites? I understand there were a great number of them in the West but they have since left; they did not comply with our regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, there were^ very
few Hutterites entered Canada; they would not number more than a hundred or two hundred all told. They have not all returned; they are still in the province of Manitoba. I repeat that during the past two years we have had an estimated average immigration-that is of people who have landed in Canada as immigrants-of 133,402. Now, going back: During the five years from 1897 to 1901, the average number of people who landed in Canada each year was only 34,240 as against 133,402 for the last two years. Taking the next five-year period, that is from 1902 to 1906, the total number of people landed in all of Canada was 661,405, or an average of 132,281, as against an average the last two years of 133,402. Now, people do not know these facts. People have an idea back in those days there was a tremendous immigration boom such as Canada has never seen since. As a matter of fact during the ten years of that period from

1897 down to 1906 the annual average for the whole ten-year period was only 83,260, as against an average during the past two years of 133,402. During the following five-year period, from 1907 down to 1911, the statistics show, the number of people who entered Canada was 1,053,922, or an average for each year of 210,784. The average during the last two years was 133,402. But, Mr. Chairman, there is a factor, and a very important factor that enters there. It is now some three or four years since every homestead in Western Canada was taken out of settlement. We could not advise a single man in the United States, or in Great Britain, that when he came to this Dominion he could get a homestead in Western Canada except those away out from the railways. Because, as a matter of fact, Parliament had agreed that there should be reserved for the soldiers all lands existing within fifteen miles,-1 think it was,-or every railway in the West. As a consequence, during the last two or three years we have not had the (privilege of inviting any people to come to Canada to get free lands as they could in the old days. Notwithstanding that fact, the comparison still shows that, although the free lands were not available, the numbers coming to Canada, in comparison to those who came in the days to which I have referred, were by no means small. If you take the full period from 1897 down to 1911-a fifteen-year period -the average immigration to Canada during the whole fifteen years amounted to 125,768 as against, again, an average of 133,402 during the last two years. The peak load of our immigration occurred in the years following 1911. And there was reason for that. In those years Canada was a booming country-we boomed as we had never boomed before. In 1912, 1913 and 1914 we received an average each year of no less than 380,515 immigrants. Then came the war.
Now, that is not the whole story. I wish to give the Committee some idea of comparative figures as to the number of immigrants from Great Britain, the United States and other countries.

Before the minister gives
those figures, could he tell us how many of the 133,000 were soldiers' wives? The statement seems remarkable to me, a Western man, for I have not seen this influx of settlers. Perhaps this might be accounted for by a large number of soldiers' wives being included in that figure.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, as a matter of fact
those figures do not include soldiers and their dependents who had not been in Canada before; these were kept entirely separate from the total. Of course, the hon. gentleman must not be surprised if large numbers of these people have not gone on the land in Western Canada-I shall refer to that a little later-and I am sure he understands the reasons why.
Now, as regards British immigration during these periods:	I am not going
over all the figures I have here, but during the fifteen year period from 1897 to 1911 the total British immigration was 723,424, or an annual average of 48,228, as against an average during the last two years of 68,001. In other words, we got on an average from Great Britain during these last two years more people than the average annual influx during that boom period about which we hear so much talk. The war did not materially affect our immigration from the United States. The everage immigration from that source during the fifteen-year period was 43,361, whereas the average during the last seven years, including the war period, was 52,549. In other words, during the last seven years we received from the United States annually 9,000 more people than during the fifteen-year period down to 1911. In addition to that it will be of interest to the Committee to know that for the eleven months of last year for which I have exact figures our settlers from the United States brought with them, according to the returns, property valued at no less than $14,425,411.61.

Has the minister given
the total from the United States for the same period?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I can give the figures.
The total from the United States for the fifteen-year period was 650,429.
And the average?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
For that fifteen-year
period, 43,361, and for the last two years, 52,549.

What class of settlers
brought in that fourteen million dollars odd?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
All classes. When a
person comes in from the United States and brings his effects, whether he be a farmer or a householder, his goods must be entered at the customs house and valued.

What amount was
brought in by other settlers during the same period?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have not those figures before me at the present time, but they would be very easily ascertainable, because a record is kept.

As a matter of fact
the minister does not deny that the great boom in the Western Provinces began in 1897?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Certainly. I said at
the outset that I did not wish to detract from the work done at that time. But there is a factor that very many people lose sight of, and that is that a very large part of the West was settled by Easterners, not by immigrants. You can scarcely go anywhere in the Prairie Provinces without meeting people from Ontario, Quebec and the Maritime Provinces. Thousands of people from Eastern Canada moved West. The West has not been filled up entirely by people coming into Canada.

But my recollection
is that those large European colonies of good immigrants, such as Galicians, Russians and other people from Central Europe, came during the period after 1897. I remember seeing long trains of such immigrants passing through Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is quite correct.
Has the minister given the total figures for the fifteen-year period?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I gave those figures to the Committee.
The hon. minister has said that a record is kept of the value of goods brought in by immigrants. Is that record kept here?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would imagine that it is kept at the seaboard. All goods passed by immigrants must be classified and a record of the total value kept by the customs authorities. I have not the figures before me, but I would think they would be very easily ascertainable.
So there is no basis of comparison available at the moment of the value of goods brought in by immigrants from other countries as against the value brought in by immigrants from the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, I have not those
figures at hand. I wish to refer for a few moments to another feature of the situa-

tion. A good many people fail to realize that conditions in Canada from the standpoint of immigration are not the same to-day as they were some years ago; they have changed very materially. Many people have an idea that there is an unlimited number of homesteads still available. That is not the case. You can draw a line across the three provinces passing through, say, Prince Albert and away north to Edmonton, and from there to the International boundary, a distance of 250 or 300 miles, there is not a homestead left that is reasonably fit for homesteading. Members who are acquainted with the western provinces will agree with me.
Not under cultivation?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not all under cultivation by any means. But at the time we were supposed to have that very heavy immigration, when the country was settled up by leaps and bounds, we had millions of acres of the finest land in the world of which a man could get 160 acres by payment of a fee oi: $10.
And then he was given the right of pre-emption on adjoining lands.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, there were provisions for pre-empting. Well that day has gone. Do not misunderstand me; I do not say that in Western Canada there are not lands that can be homesteaded, but those which are available are largely distant from railways; they are mostly in northern portions of the provinces and partly or wholly covered with timber, bush or scrub. They are not in the open prairies where a man can stick his plough in the ground and plough up 160 acres without any trouble; they are homesteads upon which capital must be invested and upon which hard work.must be done before the land is fit for farming. So that those who have the idea that we are living in the old days, so far as the West is concerned at any rate-well, they "have another guess coming." In the carrying on of its publicity work to-day the Department of Immigration is not in a position to hold out to the prospective settler the inducements that could be held out in the old days. We cannot advertise that we have all this available land for homestead purposes. That was the great drawing card in the old days; that is what brought thousands of people to this country. I know that we till have an abundance of land. The member for Maisonneuve was referring the

other day to what was taking place in the Abitibi region, and the same is true, to a more or less limited extent, along the Transcontinental, along the Canadian Northern, and in the northern parts of Saskatchewan and Alberta and Manitoba. But the condition is by no means the same as it was in the old days.
I would like the committee to bear another fact in mind, and I would like the people of Canada to understand it clearly. People say that we should adopt a vigorous immigration policy bo get people from Northern ^Europe. What is meant by the adoption of a vigorous immigration policy? It means the establishment of agencies in those countries, the putting in of men who will go round and advise the people to come to Canada; who will lecture bo them, distribute pamphlets, and do things of that kind. Well, we cannot do that.
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They simply will not let us do it. I have had that situation inquired into very carefully. It is all very well for people to say, for instance, that we should send our agents to Denmark, turn them loose there, establish half a dozen offices in that country, get our literature out in the Danish language and carry on a publicity compaign, and so on. But the people of Denmark will not let us do that sort of thing; the people of Scandinavia will not let us do it; the people of Belgium will not let us do it; nor will the people of France. Do you imagine that France wants us to send agents over there who will advise her people to come to Canada? Why, they have lost something like a million men.
More.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, I daresay, more.
Well, do you imagine that they want us to send our propagandists there to invite their people to come to Canada?

I am glad my hon.
friend brought up this point. Even before the war the French Government warned the Canadian Office in Paris not to carry on any propaganda to that end.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Quite true. We remember what occurred in Austria, where we were getting these Galician people; we remember how the Government of Austria stepped in and put an end to the publicity work that was being carried on. So those who have the idea that all the department has to do is get together a huge staff and send it to Europe for the purpose of carrying

on publicity work and propaganda to get settlers to come to Canada should realize that we simply cannot do it; that it is not possible.
I think, however, that in Poland some excellent farmers could be obtained.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is quite possible.
I have a note which I will come to shortly on that general question.
In the old days we had an office in Antwerp, if I remember rightly, and there was one in Copenhagen for a short while. We also had an agency in Paris. These were the only three agents we had on the continent, so far as I have been able to gather, prior to the period of the war. I have discussed the matter with officials of the department and they tell me that most careful inquiries indicate that the governments of these countries will not allow us to send our agents there for the purpose of drawing away their people. On the other hand, they do not take the stand that their people should not leave. If a certain number of their people want to go it is their business, and no obstacle is placed in their way, but the governments leave it to the people themselves to decide where they will go and when they will go. All we can do is welcome those who turn their thoughts this way and assist them all we can after they come here. There is one way in which we can get people from these countries and that is through the transportation companies. In Sweden, for instance, there are a number of gentlemen of that country engaged in the transportation business. When an intending immigrant goes into the office there is nothing to prevent the transportation company from advising him where to go, and we get a certain number of these people, because some of the transportation companies are interested in inducing them to come to Canada.
Now, I wish it to be clearly understood that, so far as my information goes-and I have made careful inquiries in many quarters- our Government cannot put its propagandists in those countries for the purpose of securing emigrants from them. If we take the slightest step to start anything of that kind. I have no doubt the governments of these countries would very quickly put an end to it.

I understand that the
chief objection to emigration from these countries is that their governments do not
wish to see those capable of military service leave the country. As for the others, I understand they have no serious objection.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Well, that may be. Now, just another point. The suggestion is very frequently made that we should endeavour to secure a large number of agriculturists from Great Britain. The committee is aware that the agricultural population of Great Britain comprises only about fifteen per cent of the total population. They are an industrial, not an agricultural people. At no time during the last twenty or twenty-five years have the agriculturists of Great Britain been so well off as they are now. I was over there last year and had an opportunity of visiting nearly all our agencies and in getting in touch with the situation. Wherever I went, there was no material discontent among the farming population. They are getting higher prices than ever before for everything they produce. In addition to that, farm labour has been unionized over there and they have been able to insist upon better hours, better living conditions and better wages. The conditions with respect to that field, therefore, are not the same as they were a few years ago; we cannot now attract men from the British farms as we did then. Economic conditions in Great Britain must change very materially before we shall be able to attract to Canada even a small number of British agriculturists. Now, that is a fact that is not very well known.
I come now to the question that has been raised: Whether we should admit people from Eastern and Central Europe in large numbers, even if they are farmers. At present we have a total exclusion order against the people of Germany, Austria, Bulgaria and Turkey. That order was made some two or three years ago and still remains.
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Whether or not the time has come for its removal I am not going to say. I would like to hear an expression of the views of members on that point.
How many Germans were admitted, say in the year 1912 or 1913, when immigration was very heavy? Has the minister that information?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have not those figures at hand. I would imagine that the number would be fairly heavy. At any rate, we have that exclusion order in force at the

present time. The question was raised the other day by the hon. member for Strath-cona (Mr. Douglas). He pictured certain settlements in Western Canada, settled by Russians, Austrians, Poles, Roumanians and other people of that class. I thoroughly agree with the statement.

A moment ago I mentioned Poles. Does the minister include Poles who formerly belonged to Prussian Poland amongst the Germans? When I mentioned Poles, I referred to Poles, whether they were under Russian, Prussian or Austrian rule. They are a race by themselves, and I should like the minister to believe that when I mentioned Poland, I referred to Central Europe as being a field for our immigration.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As the order stands, it would include some of the Poles. It covers, I think, the geographical area of those countries as they existed before the war. I am not, however, certain on that point.

As I understand the matter, it is just the opposite. That is to say, the whole territory that is now incorporated in Poland, is treated as part of Poland, and the inhabitants are called Polish Nationals, so that any person who is resident now in Galicia, that large country which was formerly part of Austria, is now treated as part of Poland, and immigrants from that country are free to enter.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is the rule that should be adopted. To come back, I was speaking of settlements in Western Canada composed of those people. The hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Douglas) pictured those settlements as having made very considerable progress. He stated that those people had 'added very materially to the wealth of Canada; that they were prosperous and law-abiding. With that I agree. I know those settlements well; I have known them for years; I have spent many a day in them; I have lived amongst those people, and I know what they have done.
They voted for you.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, many of them voted for me as well. You have the two views expressed. Mr. Beatty, for example, on the one hand, holds the view that those people should be admitted very freely to Canada if they are the right kind of people -farmers and others of that class. On the other hand, I am inclined to think that the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. TMr. Calder.]
Crerar) holds a different view. The quotation of his statements which I gave from the Manitoba Free Press, distinctly states that we must be very careful in admitting those people in large numbers at the present time on account of conditions in Western Canada. Those people are not of the same race; they have different ideals, different customs. It is quite true, I have no doubt, that, in the process of time they will become assimilated; but whether we should admit large numbers of those people in a comparatively short time where those three Prairie Provinces have had many difficulties in the past, is a problem that must be very carefully considered.
What-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We are in committee now and there will be plenty of opportunity for asking questions afterwards. I would prefer it if hon. members refrained from asking questions at present, because that naturally throws me off. What I was going to say is this, that down to the present time, on account of those people with their ideals, customs and ideas coming and settling in large communities together, all three provinces in Western Canada have had a great deal of trouble on their hands from the educational standpoint, the social standpoint, and that sort of thing. I think I am voicing the view of the majority of the people of Western Canada when I say that, while they consider those people to whom I refer as suitable as being farmers and from the standpoint of wealth production, and being able to succeed and to be eventually assimilated, they say: "Do not bring these people in in such numbers that they will be out of proportion to the peoplh in these provinces now; we have enough trouble on our hands at present."
What is the nature of the trouble of which the minister speaks?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I was referring particularly to the trouble which they have had in connection with their educational problem.
Is the educational problem not largely due to the Dominion Government's agreement? Did the Dominion Government not make an agreement of that kind with the Mennonites when they came in?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It has nothing to do with that at all. Just a word as to the regulations that we have put into force in order,

if possible, to check the flow of people who may be regarded as undesirable or not needed in Canada at the present time. During the progress of the previous debate, many hon. members referred to the two Orders in Council providing for certain regulations. Let me say in the first place that at the present time-and I am sure I am not exaggerating-there are in the big cities^ in the small cities and in the ports of Europe, hundreds of thousands of people awaiting entry into either Canada or the United States. Many of those people are war refugees; many of them have lost everything they had in the world, and are looking out over the world to find a new country in which they can make a home. Many of thean are penniless; they simply endeavour to scrape together what they can to get out to some new country. They are weary of Europe and all that it means to them, and they want to get away. We have set up two restrictions in an endeavour to hold back that flood. In the first place, we have increased the money qualification, and a good deal of objection was taken to that in the House the other day. The Order in Council now in force provides that, with the exception of farmers, farm labourers and domestic servants, all other classes of skilled and unskilled labourers, must have $250 in cash. In ordinary times the money qualification required is only $50.

Farm labourers are
allowed in free?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
All farm labourers, all farmers, all domestic servants, are allowed in even if they have nothing in their pocket. As regards others, if a man is accompanied by his wife, he must have $125 in addition, and if accompanied by minor children, he must have $50 in addition for each child. Hon. members can easily calculate how much money a family would have to have. The question, in a nutshell, is, whether or not we should relax. The other day when the subject was under discussion, many members said that we had a money restriction on farmers and farm labourers desirous of ccaning to Canada. That is not so, and it never has been so. We have put up the money qualification to restrict city dwellers, skilled and unskilled labour. Does any person mean to tell me that we should lower that restriction at the present time; that we should allow any man to enter Canada because he is sound in body and mind and willing to work, with nothing in his pocket; that we should allow 500 such
people to land in Toronto, 600 in Hamilton,
1,000	in Winnipeg and 2,000 in Vancouver? I doubt it very much.
I think some hon. gentlemen have an idea that this is a fixed thing. It is not fixed; it may be changed at any time. Just so soon as economic and other conditions in Canada warrant us in removing it, it can be removed. It is a matter that is entirely in the hands of the Governor in Council. But so long as conditions now prevailing continue, it seems to me, it is in the interests not only of Canada but of the immigrant himself that he should not be allowed to enter unless he has sufficient money to take care of him for a short while.

He will be
all right if he has a good pair of hands.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
But the trouble there,
as my hon. friend will realize, is who is going to decide whether he has a good pair of hands?
I decided that for myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Here are thousands of
people desirous of coming into Canada. Are we going to decide in the case of every one of them whether he has a good pair of hands? You must have a restriction of that kind, or none at all, it seems to me.

Does the immigrant
simply show the money, or must he deposit it?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He must show it.
They just come in with the money; they do not deposit it?

No, the Government
leaves them the money.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We do not take the
money from them. They simply show that they have it in their possession.

Then the same money
might be shown by several different immigrants; it might be just loaned to them for the purpose of getting in?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That would be very
difficult.

These people art very
clever.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think our officers are
just about as clever as they are in that respect.

They take after the
minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The other regulation to
which strong objection has been taken is that which requires people coming from a foreign country to come on a through ticket, by continuous passage. A man coming from Roumania, we will say, must come to Canada on a through ticket. He cannot loiter on the way, stopping off at his country and that, and finally purchase a ticket for Canada and land here. We retain the right to reject him in a case of that kind. We do not reject in every case, but we have that discretionary power. There is a reason for the existence of that regulation. Let me illustrate: During the course of the last few years thousands of people have got into the United States from foreign countries. It is very easy to cross the line into Canada. Now we use that regulation to debar people from this country who we think are not desirable. Ordinarily we admit United States citizens, but in the ease of undesirables who have got into the United States, and who desire to come into Canada, we put up this bar of the through ticket. The reason for that regulation is that a comparatively large number of persons in the United States who are not really desirable seek entry into Canada. There is another feature. If we did not have this regulation, and admitted one of these people and he afterwards turned out to be undesirable, we could not deport him to the United States, but would have to deport him to the country of origin. For instance, if he came from Bulgaria to the United States, stayed there for two or three or four months, and then crossed into Canada, if we wished to deport him we would have to send him back to Bulgaria. That is one of the reasons why this through ticket regulation has been adopted. I can see objections to it. There have been a certain number of cases of hardship, but nevertheless, from the standpoint of preventing undesirables from entering Canada. I can assure the House that it is a very useful regulation. In order to show how these two regulations have operated, I got the figures out to-day and when you see them in cold type it does not look as if any great hardship had resulted. Under the money regulation we have excluded at our ocean ports during eleven months of last year only 325 people. The number excluded at ocean ports out of some $93,701 people, because they did not have a through ticket, was only 264. On the other hand, see how these regulations operate against the great numbers of people in the United States who are [iMr. 'McMaster.]
seeking entry into Canada. There were turned back in those eleven months at boundary points intending immigrants from the United States to the number of 7,108, as against only 325 at ocean ports; and we turned back at boundary points 8,753, as against only 264 at ocean ports, because they did not have through tickets. In other words, in so far as the admission of undesirables into Canada from the United States is concerned, we find these two regulations most valuable indeed. If these regulations are to go, it seems to me there is only one thing for the House and the Government to do. Unless we are going to have some restrictions of this class or some other class, I think we will have to go back and consider what was suggested to the House some two years ago, we will have to put on a measure of total exclusion so far as certain classes are concerned; that is to say, we will have to say that certain classes of people shall not come into Canada, or that they shall only come in in limited numbers, as is now suggested by the Congress of the United States. It seems to me that we must either have a restrictive law as we have at the present time, leaving its administration largely in the hands of the Government as to the numbers that shall come in, and who shall be considered undesirable, or we must have a fixed law setting out clearly what classes of people shall not come in. I have been speaking for rather a long time-
There is no closure on this.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
-but there has been a good deal of talk on the subject of immigration in the last two or three years, and I have thought it advisable that certain aspects of it should be clearly set forth before the House and the country.
It was suggested by the hon. member for Oxford the other day that we should arrange for the selection of our immigrants in Europe, that they should be examined over there, instead of allowing them to come to our shores and making the selection here. He pointed out that the present system entailed a great deal of expense and resulted in a great deal of hardship to those who happened to be rejected. Let us look at the question for a minute. At the present time there is no country in Europe where people are not desirous of coming to Canada; I will not except one country, there are hundreds, yes thousands of people in every one of these countries who want to come to Canada. How would you make

the selection in Europe? There is only one way of doing it. We would have to establish in every country in Europe the necessary machinery before which these people would have to go. We would have to have officers there to decide which man should come to Canada, and which should not, and not from the standpoint of money alone; the health of these people would also have to be examined. It would not simply mean that we would have to have an ordinary immigration agent there; we would have to have a doctor, and not an ordinary doctor, because one of the grounds upon which we exclude people from entering Canada is mental deficiency. So if we were to examine them on the other side, we would have to have a staff of immigration officers, a staff of doctors, and a staff of mental experts, in practically every country in Europe. If the House is prepared to vote the necessary Estimates in order to establish that machinery, we can do it. We can wipe out a great deal of hardship that exists, and cause the least possible degree of inconvenience to people, if this House is ready to sanction the necessary expense. But I doubt very much whether that would be done.

The minister knows very
well that, as a matter of fact, there are only a few ports in Europe from which people come,-Liverpool, Glasgow, Havre and one or two others,

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, but suppose a man wants to come from Roumania; are you going to have him sell his home and everything that belong to him and go to Antwerp for examination by our officers and be there rejected after he has broken up his home?

But people come to
Halifax and are turned away.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It seems to me if the
problem is to be dealt with in a practical way, the steamship companies must cooperate with us and abide by our regulations. People come to Canada from all parts of Europe. We have immigrants from Greece, Italy, Spain, Portugal, and from different ports in France, and we shall have people from various ports in the Baltic; and to examine them in Europe would mean the establishment, in every one of these ports, of machinery that would include medical officers as well as ordinary agents. That would not be practicable, on the ground of expense alone. While a certain amount of hardship does exist at the present time, taking the situation
all round, I think I am safe in saying that that hardship is comparatively small. The transportation companies know our regulations; they are in touch with the immigration officers all the time, and they know the class of people we admit. So that it is largely their business to see that only the proper class of people are sent over; and if there is a small percentage of weeding out to be done, it should be done here and not in Europe.

What steps does the
department take to ensure that any man who wants to get transportation is made aware of the requirements and is denied his ticket unless he complies with certain standards which are set for these companies? Are proper steps taken in that respect?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, the widest possible
publicity has been given to that phase of the situation, and this because some hardship has resulted from the regulations. Every steamship company in the business knows what the regulations are, and, in addition to that, through the British consuls all over Europe, we have advised the various governments as to what the law is and have taken various other steps to ensure that every person, so far as is possible, shall clearly understand it. There are some people, I dare say, who do not get that information, and they should be stopped on the other side, because the steamship companies are fully aware of the law. A great deal of trouble is due to the fact that a certain number of people are in the business in Europe simply for the profits they can get out of it, and they endeavour in every way possible to evade the regulations. So that if there is any blame it is largely attributable to them.
One word with regard to another problem that stares us in the face. During the course of the last two or three or four years, I have given a good deal of study to the land question, and I have come to the conclusion that there is only one way in which it can be solved. We can go on and get a certain number of people, as we are doing now, to go on the farms in this country, but it is going to be a mighty slow process, and we shall never get anywhere so long as we pursue the policy that has obtained in the past. The days of free land are practically gone, and you cannot buy land in Western Canada to-day for less than $12, $15, $20, $25 or $30 per acre. A man who wants 160 acres of land at $20 an acre must face, first of all, a capital

expenditure of $3,200, and then there must be taken into consideration the cost of buildings, plant, horses, and everything of that kind. In the old days, a man could come from Europe and settle on the finest land within twenty miles of Regina, and start on a comparatively small sum of money. Land of the same kind is there to-day, millions of acres of it, lying in the heart of settlements all through Western Canada, but no man can go and settle on it unless he has an average capital of, shall I say, $7,000 or $6,000 or thereabouts. I daresay opinions will differ as to the amount, but I would say that on any of that land that lies there available for settlement, it would require a capital of at least $5,000 before a man could put up his buildings, get his horses and machinery, and start operations.
By whom is that land held?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mostly by speculators,
and I estimate that there is anywhere from 15,000,000 to 20,000,000 acres of it scattered over the Prairie Provinces. In my judgment, the land settlement of Canada will never take place in a large way until the State, as represented by both the federal and the provincial authorities, is prepared to step in and assist settlers financially. I hear one hon. gentleman applauding me.
Count me in, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
For how many
years?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It would vary because their laws were adopted at different times. I remember looking into this question some years ago, and I was simply astounded to find the results in one of the States, I think it was Victoria, where they had advanced millions of dollars for this work, and the records showed at the time I was making the study that they had practically not lost a single dollar as the result of their operation.
What State was that?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It was Victoria, if I
remember rightly.
How many settlers did they get?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That I cannot say. I merely wish to make this point-and probably the time is now because we have huge liabilities, we have enormous responsibilities; the fact that we have had to advance $75,000,000 for soldiers' settlement is in itself something to consider,-that in the working out of this problem in the future, if it can be done, the Federal Government and the Provincial Governments of Canada must eventually adopt some form of financial assistance to settlers or we will

never have the question solved at all. It will never be solved if we are simply going to wait for wealthy people-because to came on our farms a man must be wealthy, except in the case of fringes of land in northern Saskatchewan and Alberta; if a man is going to go into the settled regions of Canada, where there are facilities and modern conveniences, he has got to be a wealthy man in order to establish himself.
I now want to refer for a moment or two to the matter mentioned by the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) and that is the creation of the Western Canada Colonization Association. Many people have an idea that in a sense it is proposed that that association shall take the place of a department and exercise its functions. I can assure the hon. gentleman that that is not so in an sense. In my judgment there is a very distinct field of work for the new organization, brought into being by Mayor Brown of Medicine Hat and now under the management of General McRae, and I will explain the reason.
