In the old days in Western Canada land was held in large blocks by large colonization companies like the Luse Land Company, the Martin Company, the Has-lam Company, the Parsons Company, and others. These companies bought lands from the Canadian Pacific Company, or, in some cases got their lands from the Crown. They got large blocks of land containing many thousands of acres, and they carried on an extensive colonization work. They spent huge sums of money in advertising, they ran special trains all through the country, they brought thousands of visitors from the United States-they spent a great deal of money in disposing of those lands. That was quite outside of the operations of the department, which, in the meantime, was carrying on its ordinary homestead work. Well, in that respect the condition has changed; there are now only three large land owners in Western Canada to-day that we have to consider at all -the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian Northern-which I think has about 800,000 acres-and the Hudson Bay Company. The others have practically all disappeared and in their place we have a great multiplicity of small landowners,-speculators, men in towns and villages in Western Canada and in Eastern Canada, many of them living in the United States and many in Great Britain, men scattered all over the world, who hold one, or two or three sections, or fractions of sections. And that is the land that must be disposed of. These
large land companies having disappeared, and having sold their holdings to individuals, there is no person now to look after the settlement and the sale of these lands. Would any one suggest that the Government should enter that business? Do you think the department should bring into being an organization that would go down into the States to get settlers-sell John Smith's land, and John Brown's land and Tom King's land? Well if we ever wanted to get into trouble we should
5 p.m. only need to enter upon that work. It would never do in the world, the department cannot act as a selling agent. Now, I think I am quite within the mark when I state that the main reason that lies at the very bottom of the creation of this new organization is that there are these millions of acres of lands owned by private individuals that they are desirous of finding buyers for, and they are trying to bring this organization into being very largely for that purpose. I discussed the whole thing with those interested before the organization was ever formed. I thoroughly agreed with the idea they had in mind. I pointed out the difficulties that the department would have in attempting to deal with that matter in any way at all, and the result was that eventually this organization was established with the full approval of the department. We have not any doubt at all that they have a splendid work to dp and that they will do it. Now I have kept the House a long time-
Before the minister leaves that subject. He made references to 800,000 acres of land held by the Canadian Northern Railway. Are those lands vested in the State, do we own them along with the railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. Those lands came over with the other railway properties.

The minister does not
mean to imply in connection with the colonization scheme which he mentioned, that the sale of these lands is being made for the profit of the owners? The movement is in the interest of Western Canada and with a desire to promote immigration.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Oh, certainly.

I know some thing about the scheme, and I understand that the manufacturers and the merchants in Eastern Canada, largely in Quebec and Ontario, have subscribed a million and a half of dollars for that purpose, but not with the idea o{ making any profit out of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, the object was not to sell these lands in order to favour certain individuals or to make a profit out of it-that was not the idea at all. These people realize that one of the real problems of Western Canada is to find a sale for all these sections and quarter-sections that are scattered through the midst of existing settlement, and they realize that some organization would have to be brought into being for the purpose of finding a solution of .that (problem, and not for profit making at all.

The minister has made an interesting statement to which I .may or may not have something to say later. It has been very interesting but I think the minister could improve it by giving a short, succinct and compressed statement of what the present policy of the Government is in regard to immigration. We can infer a great deal from what the minister has said. He has stated a great many things, one way and another, and it is a good way , to lead to discussion, but I think the committee would like to know what is the exact policy of the Government at the present moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That can be done in a very few words. I stated it two or three times. In the first place the Government for the last three years has followed the policy of encouraging, in every way possible, three classes of people to come to Canada-the farmer, the farm labourer,, and domestics.
From where?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: From any part of the world.

Including Germany and
Austria?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The exclusion in reference to those countries is still in existence.
Including China?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: ""Few farmers come to Canada from China.
Yes, but we get domestic servants from there.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is an exclusion
at the present time against not only Chinese but all Orientals in so far as skilled and unskilled labour is concerned. Generally speaking our policy has been to foster and encourage immigration to Canada of the classes I have mentioned. In the first place, there is a limitation in so far as immigrants from enemy countries are con-
	_
cerned, which is still in operation. In the second place, so far as the Slavonic races are concerned, while we have not stopped the entry of their nationals, we have not gone out of our way to encourage them to come here during the last two or three years. As to people from the countries of Northern Europe, we encourage all three classes from those countries. As regards skilled and unskilled labour, on account of conditions existing in Canada we have not encouraged that movement; as a matter of fact we have set up restrictions debarring those people entering Canada. I do not mean that there has been total exclusion, because whenever it has been represented to the department-and the same has been true in the past and will be true to-morrow and next month-and clearly shown, that there is any class of skilled or unskilled labour not available in this country, then we seek to promote the immigration of such men. I think, in a nutshell, that covers the general ground. We have set our face against the admission for the time being of city dwellers from continental Europe. Why? Simply because they come within that class which I have mentioned, the artisan, labouring, trading, clerking class, for which there is no real need in Canada at the present time. Now, while we have done that for the time being, that is not a permanent restriction. As I have stated time and time again during the course of my remarks, it seems to me that we must take the situation as we find it and deal with it in accordance with the economic and other conditions prevailing here.
Do you allow ablebodied men from enemy countries to take up land and farm here?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They are excluded at the present time.
What effect does the minister think it would have on settlement in the Western Provinces if each province were given its natural resources and established its own system of immigration?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I doubt very much if it would make any material difference. It seems to me that the question of securing immigrants will always be for the federal authorities to deal with. I doubt very much if it would be conducive to the best interests of the provinces or of the Dominion as a whole if that work were divided instead of being centralized. Some of the

provinces already have their own representatives in London. For instance last year Ontario had Dr. Creelman over there,-a very estimable gentleman. He did splendid work, but he was in touch with our central office practically every day. This year the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan are sending over representatives, and the province of New Brunswick is sending over a lady to' work in conjunction with our London office in connection with women immigrants. I think that even if you turned back the resources to the Western Provinces the Federal authority will still have to keep hold on the general question of immigration.

Has the department
any inspectors of immigrants at the ports of embarkation?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have our port officers. At Liverpool, for example, Mr. Kerr is our agent. He and his staff have a good deal of work to do when the boats are leaving. In addition to that, we have a woman officer at that port to look after women and children. But we do not undertake to pass people on the other side. Inspection takes place at the port of entry in Canada.
Would it not be more practical if it were done on the other side?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is a large subject. We discussed it pretty fully on our Estimates two years ago. I have gone into it very fully with our own people and with the British authorities when I was over in London last year. There are many difficulties in the way, one of them being the cost of the staff which would be required. I threshed the matter out carefully with Colonel Amery, who is very much interested in something being done along that line, and we finally came to the conclusion that owing to the difficulties in the way and the cost attached to the work, things had better stand pretty much as they were. We have had one of our medical men not only in Great Britain but on the continent, and he has been working in the closest cooperation with the officials of the department and with the medical officers of the steamship companies and of the British Board of Trade. As a result the medical inspection provided by the British authorities is very much better than it was a few years ago, and comparatively few mistakes are made now. We have one of our doctors on the continent at the present time, Dr. Jeffs. In recent months we have got in touch with the medical officers of the steamship companies at Antwerp and at Havre. We are watching that end of the work very closely, but we do not undertake to give any certificates over there that will enable people to land here.

I have expressed my
views on two or three of the Orders in Council to which the minister referred this afternoon, and I have not changed those views since I spoke last. I do not want to inflict another speech upon the committtee now, they already know my views, and it would appear that the minister does not intend to have these Orders in Council revoked, at any rate for the present. .Now, this famous Order in Council which provides that any person landing in this country, other than a farm labourer or a domestic servant, must have $250 is, I can only repeat, nothing more nor less than absurd. Apparently the minister would permit all the people of Europe to land on our shores if each individual passenger had $250, and he cares not what would happen after that $250 is exhausted in living expenses. Is not that a ridiculous position? Would it not be better for the minister to accept undertakings from rela-[DOT] fives in the form of bonds or otherwise that the passenger who wishes to land will not become a public charge in any way, or will not become a factor in the labour market? All that is required under this present Order in Council is that the intending. immigrant shall have $250. With that money in his possession he is free to enter this country and work out his own salvation. Two hundred and fifty dollars seems to bulk very large in the eyes of the minister, but I have not found that it goes very far. This week we have to pay our income tax, and $250 is not a very large sum in the eyes of the income tax collector at the present moment. For the last two or three years I have brought this question of money qualification before the minister and officials of his department. Up to last November it was $50. The cost of living has gone up, and the amount has been raised to $250. The minister tells us that it is merely an Order in Council; that it can be revoked at any time, and that it probably will be revoked in the very near future when conditions are somewhat improved. Well, we expected that the fifty-dollar qualification would be taken off last fall. Instead of that it has been increased, and all we have is the promise of the minister that he will try to see his way clear to reduce it in the near future. I am not

satisfied with the minister's explanation as to the utility of this $250 requirement, regardless of whether the immigrant in question is going to be a good citizen or a bad citizen. If the immigrant can put up $250 no question is asked, he can enter.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
He does not put up the
$250.	.

Well, he exhibits it. May I point out to the minister a further absurdity with reference to this $250? If an immigrant lands at a port and a well-disposed person, a large-hearted, benevolent gentleman, comes along and is willing to hand to the immigrant $250 in order that he may have permission to enter the country, it will avail him not; he must carry the $250 in his clothes; he must have it in his possession before he lands. If any person offers him $250 in Canada, it is of no effect whatever. Now, is the department sincere in exacting this $250? Are the Government sincere in saying that it is for the purpose of seeing that the immigrant shall not become a public charge? Because if they are sincere, why not accept the money from whatever source it comes, and let the passenger land? The object would clearly seem to be to keep the passenger out of the country, and it is thought that the $250 will have that effect. Well, sometimes it does and sometimes it does not. I know that in a very large number of cases' the $250 is sent to the passenger from Canada by a relative, and the passenger lands fully qualified. But if the relative, fearing that the mails may miscarry, hands the money to the passenger at the port, then the would-be immigrant is disqualified; he is not fit to associate with good Canadian citizens. That is the position with regard to this $250. I must say that the Government are not sincere when they profess that this requirement is provided for the purpose of seeing that the person in question will not become a public charge.
Now, the other test of qualification is the non-continuous journey test, and if there is anything more absurd than the $250 qualification it is the non-continuous journey test. Take the case of a man and his family who leave Roumania, perhaps to escape persecution; perhaps because they do not like the Roumanian method of living; perhaps because they are no longer desired in that country. They go to, say, Glasgow or London and live there for fifteen years. In the meantime the little ones grow up sufficiently to attend schools

and colleges. Then the head of the family hears something about this great and glorious and wonderful country and thinks it might be better for him and his family to come to Canada. They hope to improve their condition, and after all you cannot find fault with a man who wishes to improve his condition. Well, when he lands in Canada the first question put to him is: "Where were you born?" The answer is: "Roumania." Then he is asked whether he had been absent from that country beforg coming to Canada, and if so, for how long. In this case the immigrant would say: "I left Roumania fifteen years ago and have during that time been living in London. I have brought up my children under the British system. They are now able to speak and write the English language. They are first-class Cockneys; listen to their accent." But the inspector would be very much astonished and would say: "Why, you cannot enter this country; you have not come by continuous journey." If he had come from Roumania direct; if his children were unable to speak a word of English or understand anything said to them in that language; if the family had .come from Roumania direct, with everything that that implies-I am not going to go into details here-then they would be perfectly eligible for admission into Canada. But if the man had improved his condition and that of his family by living in any of the British countries even for three months, they would not be eligible for admission to this country. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, could anything be more absurd than a rule of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Has the hon. gentleman
in mind a concrete case where a person from Roumania or any other such country, who had lived in Great Britain for a number of years and had had his children educated there, was refused admission to Canada on this ground?

Well, I have many concrete cases. If the minister wishes me to do so I will send him a list of people who have been rejected for that very reason. I admit-and I wish to do the minister justice-that when I have brought cases of this kind before him he has exercised his discretion and permitted these men to enter. I know of one case which I brought to the attention of Mr. Cory, deputy minister of the Interior. It was the case of a man going to Hamilton. I think the name was Berg.
Burglar?

No. He could have be-'
come that, though, after he had lived a little while in Hamilton. When I went to Mr. Cory about this case he, the deputy minister, was a berg-an iceberg-in the matter of admitting the man into Canada. Finally I appealed to his common sense, to his higher reason, and so on. He told me that if I persisted in bringing cases of that kind before him so frequently it would probably affect his position and might to a certain extent affect mine. But it was only through pure good-will on the part of Mr. Cory that this particular family was permitted to enter. There were three or four children and the family had lived in England for fifteen years-that was the case I had in mind. But there are numerous other instances which I could mention. If this regulation is established by Order in Council and is not enforced, why not abolish it altogether? Now, the minister told us to-day that only about three hundred people had been rejected because they did not have the money qualification.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: At the ocean ports.

Well, it seems to me
that I have been in the minister's room at least six hundred times on cases of that kind. Perhaps he has carefully suppressed my cases from the files; I do not know. Certainly there seem to have been more than three hundred cases. But every immigrant realizes that he must come to this country with the $250 tied up in his sock or sewn into his clothes; he knows that he cannot enter unless he has that amount. In a number of cases the poor wretch has been short six or seven dollars. Probably he had to bribe an official in Antwerp or in some other European town in order to get decent treatment. Or perhaps the pangs of hunger were a little too strong and he had to use a little of the money; therefore when he landed he did not have the full amount and was turned back. In some cases the money had been stolen from these people. They realize, however, that it is vital that they should have the $250, and that is why so few of them have been sent back through lack of that qualification. But as to the non-con tinuous journey qualification, it is almost impossible to avoid non-compliance. If a man has been born in Roumania and has lived in England for twelve or fifteen years, he cannot qualify. It is said that even God Almighty cannot make Monday out of Sunday,-it is somewhat the same
with the immigrant; he simply cannot help it. It was a position which he could not overcome at all. That is how many of those people-about 8,000, I am told,- were rejected on account of non-continuous journey. I should like to point this out to the committee:	in the United States
there is nothing corresponding to the Orders in Council which we have here as regards non-continuous journey and the money test. Is it not strange that the United States, with a population of 110,000,000, have not a single rule with regard to stopping a passenger at a port, unless he suffers from a loathsome disease or is disqualified by reason of health? If a man has a vise from the American Consul in the place from which he started, that is sufficient and he is allowed to land in the United States. There you have a country with a population of 110,000,000 and no objection to allowing people to enter, and here with our paltry eight or nine million people, we turn up our noses and are more particular.	_
The minister stated that if a man is destined for a farm, or if a woman is a domestic servant, they can enter; they need not have a single penny in their pocket. Why is_ that? The minister told us a few minutes ago that no person can hope to make a success on the farm unless he has five, six or seven thousand dollars. Otherwise the task is a hopeless one. So it is. How can a person going to Western Canada hope to be a success if he is penniless? All he can do is to become a farm labourer. The woman must be a domestic servant before she can be allowed to enter. If she is skilled with her fingers, if she can become a modiste or seamstress or milliner, she is debarred. The man must be a farm labourer and the woman a domestic servant. We want to turn people into hewers of wood and drawers of water and then they will be eligible. What kind of people are you going to have if rules of that kind are imposed for a number of years? Every person who comes into Canada will have to be in the class that I have mentioned or he or she will not be permitted to enter. Why not allow Germans and Austrians to come into this country as farm hands or domestic servants? Surely they are good enough to work for us. The Israelites under the old law turned their enemies into hewers of wood and drawers of water and they were a great success as such. Let our former enemies be our slaves at any rate and they may

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
pay off some of the indemnity which we are promised and probably will never get.
The minister spoke about assisting farmers to go on the land. That is a splendid scheme! It would run into tens of millions of dollars. Are we in a position to do that just now? I do not think we are. I have in mind the case of the Baron de Hirseh Trust, a Jewish organization in Europe which has a number of colonies in the West, four or five thousand colonists. They started to work about twenty-five or thirty years ago and they have maintained these colonists. They have taken them from the cities,-city dwellers, as the minister says -and they have turned them into very successful farmers in the West. But they have done that at an immense cost. Those people are charged 4 per cent for the money which is advanced to them, and in many cases where they cannot pay, further sums are advanced to them, even without interest, and they are kept on the land. But it is a long story, and it has been a success only to a certain" extent. It shows, however, that the thing can be done.
The minister says: We do not want city dwellers; we do not want people who are skilled artisans; we want farmers. I tell the minister that the only way you can get people to go on the land is to make it profitable for them to be on the land. If a man finds that he is going to do better on the farm than he can in the city, he is going to go on the farm. But as long as you get people to go into the cities and they earn large salaries and live in slums in the glare of the gas-light and so on, without making farm life pleasant and comfortable, so long will you have cities filled with people of that kind and you will have no people on the farms at all. Make farm life comfortable and pleasant, and then it follows, as the day the night, that people will leave the cities and settle once more in the country. But that is not going to be done in a day. I say again that even without making farm life as comfortable and pleasant as it should be, where you have in the cities a condition where men cannot obtain employment at all, where they are working for one day and for three days they are doing nothing, so that they are on the verge of starvation, and where on the other hand you have positions vacant on the farm where they can obtain employment, these people will naturally gravitate to the farms because there is nothing which drives a person to do work which he does not care for like hunger, and he will eventually find his way on to the farm.

The artificial rules which the department makes do not appeal to me, and I do not think they appeal to any person of common sense. They are certainly artificial rules, and I do not think that they are working effectively to-day. I do not think they are working with all these restrictions that are being imposed. The undesirable immigrant who wants to come into this country will come in notwithstanding any rules which the minister may make. He will find his way in by the underground route, and that is a way which is very effective. If all these people whom we brought into this country were examined, as I am sure they were, at the ports of entry, to find out whether they were free from anarchism, bolshevism and all other isms, how is it that you have in Canada conditions such as we have had within the past year or two. Surely, these people never grew up in Canada. They came from the other side, the leaders actually came from the British Isles, and they were the fomentors of the discord in this country which has been deplored so much by the Government.
I do not know that anything that I have said has any character of freshness about it, but if it is the truth, I want to hammer it in as often as I can and I trust that in time the minister will see that perhaps after all these orders in council to which we have taken such serious objection will be finally repealed.

Just by way of endorsing and enforcing what my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) has said, as regards the importance of making farming profitable and attractive, I should like to ask the minister (Mr. Calder) if he has seen the statement of a late colleague of his, Mr. Langley, which statement appeared in the press a day or two ago, that a number of farmers in the province of Saskatchewan are destitute at the present moment? That is a very serious statement. My hon. friend knows Mr. Langley very well. Mr. Langley is a man of strong and intelligent mind, and I cannot think that he would make a statement like that without having some ground for it. If there be any truth in Mr. Langley's statement, I should like to point out that that state of affairs has a very important bearing on the policy which, the minister says, the Government were enthusiastically in favour of, and that is bringing people to Canada at the present time to put them on farms. It seems a rather doubtful line of policy to encourage people to come from

foreign countries to engage in an occupation in which those already inhabiting the country, in the minister's own province, are destitute, according to the testimony of a former colleague of his in the Saskatchewan Government. I need scarcely point out to the minister that the same statement, if true, ought to make him more than cautious about embarking upon a policy of assisting people who are going to farm. That is a very doubtful project to my mind. I think that we should do well to see our soldiers through for a little while before we embark, as a country, upon any larger scheme of encouraging land settlement. I should like the minister's views on these two points in view of the statement of his colleague. Out there we all know that with the present railroad rates and the drop in prices farming in Western Canada is no picnic at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I know Mr. Langley
very well, and I think my hon. friend from Red Deer knows him well. He is sometimes inclined to draw the long bow when in his judgment there is a good occasion to do so. What Mr. Langley said, so far as conditions in certain portions of Saskatchewan are concerned, is quite true. There is a section of Saskatchewan, and a portion of Alberta, where they have had a series of dry years, and where in consequence the conditions are far from being satisfactory. But to say that the farmers generally are in a destitute condition-well, I not only doubt the statement, but I know that it is not a fact.

I did not
understand Mr. Langley to say that, nor did I quote him. I said that some farmers were destitute.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If you look over the
record, and the facts can be easily ascertained, you will find that as a class the farmers of the western provinces generally, speaking, as a result of the last four or five years' operations, are better off than they ever were before.

War prices,
of course.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not speaking of
present prices. I say that the financial standing of the farmers as a class to-day is in my judgment much better than it has been for years. It is quite true that prices have dropped, and that many farmers are in difficulties as a result. I dare say that many of them did not make
their farming operations pay last year on account of the cost of labour and falling prices, but I doubt very much if we should cease our efforts to induce farmers to come to Canada merely because of a more or less temporary local condition.
Then, as regards the other question. Notwithstanding what my hon. friend says, he hesitates about embarking upon any scheme of financial assistance for farmers. I quite understand his viewpoint. I have hesitated myself even to recommend it to the Government. But I do say this, after a very careful and a pretty thorough study of the whole situation: Canada will not solve its land settlement problem in a big way until the state is prepared to assist. That is my view; I may be wrong but that is the conclusion I have come to. Take my hon. friend's own province, for example. All around Calgary, and Red Deer, and Wetaskiwin, there are large areas where /there are Hands for sale. Where are you going to get the people to go on those lands? You have to wait for the wealthy men to come. As I stated in my main argument, there are hundreds of thousands of people, able-bodied, well-trained, thoroughly capable men, who would go on the land and make splendid settlers if they had the means, but they have not, and it seems to me it is the duty of the state in the interests of the general prosperity of the country, not of the individual, to see that these men should be brought in contact with the land and the land developed. That can only be done by some kind of government assistance. Wealthy people who are well-established in other countries are not going to come to Canada,-I am speaking now generally. They are not the kind of people you are going to get, for they are doing well; they are satisfied; they have got what they want. It seems to me we must adopt some plan of state assistance in land settlement, or I fear that the problem will go on until little by little we get the country gradually settled, but that will be a very slow process. I do not say the time is ripe now, but eventually some scheme of state assistance will have to be adopted.

May I point out that many of these land companies are quite willing to sell their lands on crop payments. Were the conditions made favourable enough, does not the minister think that a great many of these people would come ifi and take up land on such terms?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
A good many of them have come in in that way. The company

still operating has brought in a fairly large number of people. They sold the land on crop payments and that is how they are operating at the present time. But you must remember that these land companies have disposed of their holdings in the main. The lands in Western Canada that are awaiting settlement-we should not be discussing Western Canada alone, because this is an Eastern Canada problem as well-are not, in the main, held by large companies, but by individuals. I own some myself. I would be glad to sell to-morrow. And there are thousands like myself who own half a section or a section of land.
I would tax the minister.	-
Those lands might be made available on crop payments.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: But the trouble with individuals like myself is that we have not the means or the desire to be bothered with finding a buyer. I go on with my other business, but if some one asked me to sell, I would be prepared to sell. There are millions of acres of land held by private individuals the world over, who would be willing to sell, but there is no organization for getting them in touch with buyers. That is one of the main reasons for the creation of that association I have referred to.

Suppose a man from Roumania were to come to New York city, remain there for a year or so, and then make up his mind to settle in Canada; he would probably be turned back. Suppose he is turned back, goes bock to Roumania, and then after a while bids good-bye to his cousins there and comes direct to Canada ; would he be allowed to enter this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In the former case he
would not be coming by continuous passage. Our inspectors all along the border must exercise their own judgment whether an immigrant should be admitted.
What is the underlying principle?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
To admit farmers and
classes of people who are desired in this country. If this man was a mechanic, under present conditions in Canada, we would invoke the non-oontinuous passage regulation to shut him out. If we required lots of labour, and he was a labourer, we would let him come in. As I pointed out

before, if we allowed an immigrant from the United States to enter Canada, and he becomes an undesirable, we could not deport him to the United States, but we would have to pay the expense of taking him all the way back to Roumania. The Order in Council is used simply as a means of securing an end. We could waive it at any time. If a man is not of a class that we want to admit to Canada, and he does not come by continuous passage, he may be rejected, but if he is a farmer, we will suppose, he may appeal and we have power to let him in. This regulation is used simply as a means to shut out undersirables.

In the last few years I
have had considerable to do with the Department of Immigration with regard to the cases of intending immigrants. I do not say that the doors should be thrown open entirely at this particular time for the admission of all kinds of people from various countries. The department was probably justified in maintaining, at least during the winter, some restrictions in regard to skilled labour; but I do associate myself with the protests made by the member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs), with regard to two regulations, namely, the money qualifications of $250 for adult male immigrants, and the other regulation with regard to continuous passage from the country of origin. I think the money regulations is inadvisable. If an otherwise desirable person has all the qualifications or, if you prefer, the potentialities of good Canadian citizenship, the department should not exclude him merely because he is poor.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is a point in connection with the money qualification which I did not explain, and which has not so far been brought out in the discussion. It is not necessary that every man who enters should have $250. In that respect there is a discretion which has been exercised, and only within the last few days I had the case of a man who had only $190. If a man is of the right class, the class we need, and one whom it is not desirable to debar, we do not refuse him admission because he has not the $250.

May I suggest that if
he is of the class you need, he really does not require to have a cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That may be.

I had not heard that any discretion was exercised at all. In any case, the minister says that in the case of

farmers or domestic employees, the money qualification is not demanded. Well, I should like to know how the immigration authorities can distinguish, at the port of entry, between a man who is a farmer and a man who is an artisan. Do they simply take the man's word for it that he is going on a farm and let him in? In that event it would be easy to evade the money qualification. Apart from that, however, I do not believe in the principle of insisting that a man who otherwise has all the qualifications for becoming a good Canadian should have this amount of money. The statement of the minister as to the use of discretion is satisfactory as far as it goes, but I think that if it is desired to keep certain people out of the country for reasons other than poverty, those reasons should he stated and no one should be kept out for some reason that is after all only an excuse for excluding him. Let me say that a good many desirable citizens of Canada to-day, and men who are the forefathers, or even the fathers of gentlemen sitting in this House, would have been excluded from this country under conditions as we have them now. This country to-day needs immigration in a greater degree than ever in the past; yet the Government makes the requirements more onerous.
The other regulation to which my hon. friend referred is the one in regard to continuous passage from the country of origin. The minister asked for a concrete case, and one was given which showed what an unfair regulation this is in its enforcement. I think I could give a better one, better because actual, than the imaginary case of the Roumanian who had lived in London and whose children had been brought up to speak the English language, yet could not come to Canada, while persons coming direct from Roumania would be admitted.

It was not an imaginary
case; it was one on file.

So much the worse. It
is only a few weeks ago since I called the attention of the department to the case of a man who had come to Canada some ten or eleven years ago,-it may be longer, probably twelve or thirteen years ago- and who nad never become naturalized. I think he was of Polish origin, but he was never naturalized here. He was married in Canada and had several children born here. He went to the United States, where he did not find it difficult to enter although not coming directly from the country of
origin. His children have been educated in the schools of the United States, and a few months ago this man with his family, several of the children of which were Canadian born, tried to return to Canada. He could not get in at all; he was turned back at the border, as were some 8,000 other people who tried to get in here from the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What was his occupation?
He was a tanner, returning to his old job in Kitchener.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Were there lots of tanners looking for employment there?

I have not heard of any; in fact, there is little unemployment in my city for a reason which is not far to seek; it is the best city in Canada. However, that is merely by the way. Now, I could give another instance where the regulation worked a great hardship on worthy people.
I know of a family which desired to come from Russia. As is well known, conditions in Russia are very much disturbed, and these people were in actual danger of their lives. They lived close to the boundary and fled into what is now a part of Poland. They had not themselves the money qualification but they had friends in my city who were willing to advance them that money, as they actually did. For a time however, until the matter was adjusted by the department, and for which I wish to give commendation, there was a doubt raised as to whether they could be admitted into Canada. Why? Merely because of the continuous passage regulation. If they came from Poland, they would not be allowed to enter Canada, not coming in continuous passage from the land in which they were born. However, that matter has now been adjusted. I think the Government would be acting in the interests of the country if they removed these restrictions almost entirely.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
You add the word
"almost".

Yes. I realize that reasonable regulations must remain. I know that the department says that one reason for the regulation is that in the case of people admitted, we will say, from the United States, who originally came from Russia, if it is discovered after two or three years that they are not suitable to Canada, they may not be deported to the States, but must go back to their country

of origin. I do not see where the Government would be losing anything by that, because, if these people had come to Canada from the country of origin in the first place, they would have to be deported back to that country in any case, and the Government would not have to do anything more expensive in the way of deportation if they allowed them in from the United States or from some other intermediary country.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is just one point in connection with that. The transportation companies, knowing the rules that are now in force, endeavour to make certain that the people who come over are of such a class that they will not be deported or rejected. We throw the onus upon them. They know what the rule is, and in the main now, so far as continentals are concerned, it has worked satisfactorily. As a consequence of this rule a greater responsibility is thrown upon the transportation companies.
They have to pay the costs of. deportation.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
As a matter of fact, in the case of the 8,000 turned back-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I was referring to
Europe.
Yes, but there were 8,000 who tried to come here from the United States and were turned back either under the continuous passage regulation or because they did not have the $250.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There were about 16,000 all told.
Well, that makes it worse. Is it not a fact that these people had to run the gauntlet of the immigration laws of the United States before coming here?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They may have been
there two or three years.

Well, in that case they must have become to a certain extent americanized and accustomed to our western civilization. For that reason I believe that if they became accustomed to American ways, they might be more desirable than when they first entered the United States. But we exclude them on account of these regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Probably if the hon. gentleman saw them he would not be so sure as to that.
[Mr. Euler. 1

I should think that if they had been in the United States for some years the probability, at least, is that they have become somewhat accustomed to our ways and more assimilable in Canada. There is one other point to which I would refer. The minister spoke concerning the probability of the admission of men from former enemy alien countries at the present time. I asked him the question as to how many Germans had been admitted just prior to the war, because at that time immigration was very heavy. I think he stated in the course of his remarks that these people had been very worthy settlers in the West. Of my own knowledge I can say that the people of these races wherever they have settled in Canada-notwithstanding what we may say about the war-have developed into excellent citizens, industrious, thrifty and honest. I do not know what is in the Government's mind as to the ultimate readmission of these people, but I want to ask a question in that regard. I realize fully that there will be for a time some prejudice against these people, which, under the circumstances, is natural. But I would like to ask the minister whether, in his opinion, their admission to this country-whether it be sooner or later-would in any way prejudice the interests of Canada, except for the feeling of bitterness and antipathy towards them on account of the war. Apart from that altogether, I think that ultimately the minister and the country will find that their exclusion deprives this country of productive workers, capable of developing into good citizens, together with their children. I know, and I think the minister will bear me out in the statement, that the children of these people-taught in our public schools-which they must attend and do attend-will become the best of Canadians. There is absolutely no doubt of that in my mind and there should not be in the mind of any one else who knows them.
Hear, hear.

While the continued exclusion of recent enemy aliens may be deemed advisable for a time, because of a certain natural feeling, I believe, after all, it is a pity that such should be the case. If we could have them we would find that they are most industrious and stable, and in the majority of ways, desirable people in a country that is in dire need of people who are not afraid to work and from whom there is nothing to fear. I do not desire to press the matter, but do express the

hope that the present regulations may be modified at no very distant date.
At Six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at Eight o'clock.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
FROM THE SENATE!-SECOND READING
Bill No. 106 for the relief of Fergus McKee.-Mr. Fripp.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: House again in Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee
rose at six o'clock we were considering item No. 8 on page 83 of the Estimates, Immigration and Colonization, salaries and contingencies. The item had been under consideration since half-past three. Shall the item carry?

Mr. Chairman, before six
o'clock the minister explained the working of the Immigration Society which was formed in the West, and, as l had opened the question, I wish to say that his explanation was reasonably satisfactory.
I gathered from the minister's statement this afternoon that he had almost reached the conclusion that if we were to have a return of the days when people were flocking into our country and settling on the land it would be necessary to evolve some system to assist this class of settlers, and that he had in mind that such a system to be at all useful would run from $2,000 to $5,000 per settler. I understood the minister to say that in the western provinces there were millions of acres of idle land not too far from railway facilities, and that to a very large extent this land was held by land companies or speculators. Now, it occurred to me that to subsidize the man going on the land was rather a policy to help the speculator get rid of his land. The minister shakes his head, but in the last analysis that is how it works out. The experience of Canada from 1900 to 1914 is ample proof that it is not necessary to subsidize the settler to go upon the land. All that is necessary is to create conditions which will enable him to get a fair remuneration for his labour on the land, and thus satisfy him.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to intervene? A subsidy is
a grant. I never suggested that in any sense at all.

No, the minister advocated
a loan. But I am leading up to prove to him that in past years it was not necessary to have such a policy; indeed, the policy of Canada was not even to assist immigrants to come to this country. I have in my hand a pamphlet issued by the Immigration Department, entitled Facts and Figures of Immigration, published in 1912, when the Hon. Robert Rogers was Minister of the Interior. At the end of this pamphlet is contained certain information for intending settlers, and clause 5 informs him:
The Dominion Government does not make loans of money, stock, implements or settlers' effects to immigrants in order to enable them to start farming in Canada.
That was the policy during those years. What was the result? Those were the years of our greatest immigration. People were coming into this country at the rate of over a thousand a day seeking homes, principally in Western Canada. Many of those immigrants were people of means. They were tired of conditions in the Old World where they were discouraged by the excessive taxation and the continued demands for greater armaments, and looking about for a country in which to settle down and improve their condition, they naturally turned to Canada. In those days Canada was a land of promise to such people. The best immigration agent that we had then, and the best that we can establish to-day, is a satisfied settler.
Hear, hear.

He is the best immigration agent because he sends back word to his friends and relatives at home who are not doing very well: Gather up what you have and come to Canada where there is a field for your labour, and where you can build up a prosperous home for yourselves and your children.
Now, I submit to the minister that one of the first needs of to-day is to restore conditions to approximately what we enjoyed in those days of peace and plenty, and one of the first requisites to that end is to reduce taxation, and the high cost of transportation. Our very high freight rates after all do not strike the eastern farmer so severely as they do the farmer in the West, who has to pay transportation costs on a long haul before his products reach the seaboard. The present tax upon the products of the western farmer in the

form of high freight rates is undoubtedly a very great discouragement to the development of that part of the Dominion, and I submit to the minister that if he wishes to restore confidence and to create conditions that will make the western farmer satisfied and induce immigrants to go on our idle land and cultivate it, he must devote his energies and his talents to bringing about such conditions as will approximate those which obtained so far as freight rates are concerned prior to the recent advances granted to the railway companies. The records show that our greatest period of immigration, as I have already said, was from 1900 to 1914. Does the minister con-tra'dict that statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

Well, I will quote him some figures. The steadily increasing stream of immigration to this country between 1900 and 1914 is shown by this record: 1900, 23,000-I am leaving out the odd figures; 1901, 49,000; 1902, 67,000; 1903, 128,000; 1904, 130,000; 1905, 146,000; 1906, 189,000; 1907, 262,000; 1908, 146,000-a decrease; but by 1912-1913 the figures jumped up to 402,000. Does the minister say that we have had any greater immigration since that period? I fancy my hon. friend will not contradict that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend mentioned a fourteen year period-from 1900 to 1914. As a matter of fact, the peak load of our immigration was during the years 1912, 1913, and 1914.
Yes, that is quite correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Three years is a very different period from fourteen years.

I do not know that I need take up the time of the committee in giving the figures with regard to the cost of that immigration, but I think that the minister will admit that the cost during those years was comparatively small as compared with the cost of immigration to-day. I shall not follow that feature of it, but conditions have changed; the cost of transportation has increased, and also the cost of help. The policy of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in establishing ready-made farms -fifty in all-brought about such conditions that hundreds of persons presented themselves at the immigration agency of that company seeking to buy lands and to pay cash for them. Conditions in England to-day must be even better, so far as immigration to Canada is concerned, than 
they were in those days, because taxes in the Old Land, though high in those days, have since enormously increased. I submit that if the minister can bring about conditions in Canada whereby the man who goes on the land will get fair remuneration for his labour, there will be no need of subsidies, no need of advancing money to settlers to enable them to go upon the land. At a time when New Zealand was advancing money to settlers Canada was getting all the settlers she could take care of without offering any such advances. If we devote our energies to the restoration of sound, normal conditions under which the people will not have to pay out too much for their labour, for taxes and for transportation, we shall be in just as good a position with respect to immigration as we were in those years to which reference has been made. I hope that my hon. friend will make haste slowly in the matter of introducing any scheme that will help speculators to dispose of their lands under conditions highly advantageous to themselves. The best way to deal with this matter is for the provinces to tax idle lands so that it will be unprofitable for speculators to hold them idle; then the settlers will be able to buy them at fairly reasonable prices, go upon the land, and produce.

I wish to say a few
words upon this subject, with particular reference to one phase of immigration. But first let me express very briefly my views on the subject of immigration generally. Canada can absorb and will welcome all the bona fide settlers who care to come to her shores. We should exercise great care, however, in admitting the type of immigrant a large number of whom came to Canada in years gone by. I should not like to be too specific in that regard, but I will give expression to a view which has been widely held in this connection-generally speaking we should seek our immigration in northern Europe, not in the Balkan States, in extreme sourthern Europe or in Asia. That is all I care to say on the general question. But I do wish to address a few words to the committee in connection with the type of immigrant with which we on the Pacific coast are more particularly concerned. It is a question which in the last few months, for many reasons, has been assuming very serious proportions, and it is one Which I think might well engage the attention of the Government and of Parliament at this time, before the problem becomes even more acute

than it is. I refer generally to what is known as the oriental immigration problem.
For many years we have had very severe restrictions on oriental immigration. I shall not go into the details; the matter has been discussed in the House on many occasions and most of the members are pretty familiar with it. It would be too long a story to inflict upon the committee at this time; I shall simply deal as briefly as possible with some of the most imminent features of it.
I say that we have had some strict regulations regarding this immigration; yet it is true that those regulations, particularly during the last ten years, have been evaded in one manner or the other and a considerable amount of Asiatic immigration has taken place. Let me speak for a moment of the Chinese immigration. Whatever I say regarding the Chinese or the Japanese is not with any racial prejudice; my remarks are based upon exceedingly sound economic grounds and reasons. In connection with Chinese immigration we did admit students, recognizing that it was a desirable thing that Chinese students should have the advantage of western education. We did that freely, but we found that a very large number were entering as students, and immediately upon obtaining access to the country they were abandoning their scholastic pursuits and taking up different forms of labour. A few years ago, therefore, the restrictions in that regard were made more stringent. Then we admitted Chinese merchants, recognizing the desirability of promoting trade. To the amazement of the department and of all who had given study to this problem, it was found that the number of Chinese merchants entering Canada suddenly rose from three or four in a year to three or four hundred and then to over a thousand, showing that a loophole in the regulations had been discovered and taken advantage of. Now without going into any more detail, I want to say this bo the minister, very clearly and very firmly:	in my estimation-and in this I
think I correctly interpret the minds of the people on the Pacific coast who understand the problem very well and who are constantly brought into contact with it- these evasions on the part of the Chinese constitute sufficient reason, for the issuance, at least for the time being, of an exclusion order against Chinese immigration, with the possible exception of business men, tourists, and others of that character. But it would seem desirabe that immigration from China should be stopped for the time being, the attention of the Chinese authorities being drawn to the fact that they have deliberately evaded our regulations where we endeavoured to treat them reasonably, and thus secured entry for large numbers under false terms.
The Japanese immigration situation has been controlled very largely under regulations or agreements entered into between the Laurier Government and the Japanese Government, and brought about by a mission undertaken by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), whereby the Japanese Government voluntarily restrict their immigration. In this regard, however, while the immigration has been kept pretty well within bounds, there are evidence that the understanding has, perhaps, been somewhat strained. I do not have very serious complaint as to the number that come in; I think they did strain the number somewhat, but not very seriously, though sufficiently, I believe, for the Government to give to the Japanese Government a warning that they must scrupulously observe their agreement; otherwise, we shall do what I have suggested in connection with the Chinese, namely, put on a complete exclusion order.
Let me turn to another point in connection with Japanese immigration in particular. There was a recent test case in British Columbia, when a provincial law which was passed in connection with the employment of coolies on Government contracts in British Columbia-I have forgotten the details of it,-was declared ultra vires by the Supreme Court and the Privy Council, because it was in violation of the spirit or terms of the Anglo-Japanese Treaty, and I desire to take this opportunity of urging upon the minister that, in the consideration of the renewal of this treaty during the coming year, Canada should not only reserve, as she did before, the right to control her immigration, but go further than that and reserve absolute right to control not only immigration into Canada, but the dealing with the citizens or the nationals of Japan while they are in Canada. I will give the reason for this. Within the last five years there has developed in British Columbia, as in California and other Pacific coast states, a problem which is becoming so acute that, it matters not whether this Government or Parliament take cognizance of it now or not, they will certainly take cognizance of it before long. The part of wisdom is to take cognizance of it now. What I say as regards British Columbia applies to Cali-

fornia and other States. The problem is this. There are in my province districts which have been settled for twenty, thirty, or forty years, the choicest districts in British Columbia, fruit growing districts, districts intensively cultivated for the production of vegetables and so forth. Three or four Japanese or Chinese will come in and buy a piece of land, we will say, 1,000 or 100 or 300 or 400 acres, and will pay almost any price for it. Immediately that little group of orientals settles in the centre of that district, the land adjoining depreciates in value, and they buy that cheaply and thus the colony spreads. They will work their coolies from daylight to dark; they work them under conditions under which no self-respecting white man can live or dare to live, and under conditions under which we as a Parliament would not expect and would, indeed, scarcely permit, any of our people to live, Therefore, it is impossible for our people to compete with them under those conditions, and furthermore, it is not reasonable to ask our people to live alongside of communities under such conditions of life as I have indicated.
We hold in British Columbia that it is the duty of the authorities-I will come to the question of whose duty it is in a moment-to make it impossible for these orientals to hold land by ownership or by lease. That may sound very drastic, and I was approached not long ago-I have no hesitancy in making the statement here, because we might as well be frank about the question-by the Japanese Consul who asked me if this question was likely to come up regarding Japanese holding land in British Columbia, as it has come up and been legislated on in California. I told him that I did not know whether it would come up or not; but I suggested to him that it should not be a very difficult question to solve because the Japanese Government could not possibly object to our passing the same laws and regulations regarding settlers in Canada as they in Japan pass regarding settlers in that country. This seemed to embarrass him somewhat, for this reason. No Canadian is allowed to buy or own land or settle in Japan; they will not allow the foreigner to take up land there. Therefore, it is not unreasonable for us to pass in Canada a law or regulation similar to that which obtains in regard to our own nationals in) Japan. That appeals to me as sound logic, aside altogether from the merits of the case or the very serious problem which I have rather

sketchily outlined to the committee. The question arises-and this has been a political football for years:	under whose
jurisdiction does such a law come? It has been contended that inasmuch as the British North America Act specifically gives to the provinces exclusive jurisdiction in matters of property and civil rig-hts, it is within the jurisdiction of the province. That has been my opinion for many years; but while I have not under my hand a letter from the Justice Department, I am going to state to the committee a matter which can be verified, and that is that it is the opinion of the Justice Department that inasmuch as there is a treaty between Japan and Canada, legislation as regards Japanese nationals is within the prerogative of Parliament only and not within that of the province. That is borne out by the Privy Council case which I referred to a moment ago. In other words, it is the duty of this Parliament to legislate on the question of Japanese nationals holding or leasing land in any province or in the Dominion at large.
Does the hon. member say that he has an opinion of the Department of Justice to the effect that we can legislate in reference to property and civil rights?

I did not say that. I
said that there is an opinion from the Justice Department which I have downstairs in my office-I should have it here- in which they state, that inasmuch as there was a treaty, it was not within the right of the province to legislate, and the matter would he one to be dealt with by Parliament. I was going to refer to the point raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie). It may be that in face of the treaty it may not be possible for this Parliament to legislate. Therefore, what I have already said to the minister has double force, and I ask the minister to take cognizance of this point and see to it that the right of Canada in reference to legislation, as regards both immigration and the holding of land in Canada, shall be kept free from any entanglements in the treaty. In this connection if I chose to take up the time of the committee, I could bring before it an opinion by Joseph Chamberlain expressed many years ago when Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his Government first had this question up. The Eight Hon. Mr

Chamberlain who was then Secretary of State for the Colonies, if I remember correctly, gave expression to the opinion that Canada should reserve just the rights I have mentioned. Therefore, in doing so, we are not conflicting with any policy that has been held in the Motherland, at least up to the present time.
Another point which I bring to the attention of the House is this, and in doing so I shall refer to an article I saw in one of the eastern papers the other day; I think it was the Montreal Gazette. A certain clergyman said in that article that British Columbia would fall to pieces economically without Oriental labour. That is an utterly false economic doctrine. I shall not analyse it or attempt to refute it in detail, because it would take some time, but I do want to state this to the committee, which will be obvious as soon as I menion it: Orientals never have pioneered, and never will. I want the committee to get that point, because in a country like Canada I think the acid test of the value of an immigrant is whether or not he is prepared to help in the work of opening up this country- pioneering, as we call it. Now the Oriental never pioneers. He never has in any country. If you go into any of your eastern cities, you will find him in the heart of the city, and in the cities of the West it is the same. When it comes to agriculture or horticulture, you will find that the Oriental goes into a district that has been settled for years, where markets are established, and where the industry is not only established but prosperous. There he will acquire land, and as I have already mentioned, gradually eliminate those in the neighbourhood and secure control of the market. That is his method. I do not blame him for it, but I say that we are a foolish people if we allow a type of immigrant into Canada who does not contribute to the opening up of the undeveloped new districts of this country.
Another point to which I wish to direct attention is the question of assimilation. I lay this down, and I bring it to the attention of the minister and his department, as an absolutely fundamental doctrine in connection with the building up of a country, that an immigrant is only valuable to the extent that he is capable of being assimilated with the population of the country. That is a fundamental doctrine, I contend, that we cannot escape. I go further. I say we are not only justified, but it is our duty to reject immigrants who are
incapable of assimilation. Generations of experience on the Pacific coast, as well as the experience of innumerable other countries, shows beyond all peradventure that Orientals, and the Chinese in particular, cannot be assimilated. They are not assimilating, and they do not assimilate. I have but to refer hon. members who have visited the Pacific coast to San Francisco, where there are Chinese of the second and third generations, some of them intermarried with whites, and their national traits and characteristics are still there distinct and clear. Indeed I will say this, and I say it advisedly; if anything, the offspring of an intermarriage between an Oriental and a white invariably results in a lower and inferior type than either of the parent races. I have had some considerable experience in watching this in other countries, as well as in Canada and the United States, and that is invariably the case. So I say to the committee, on the question of assimilation not only as regards Oriental immigration but immigration from parts of Europe as well, we should lay it down as a principle to be followed by the Immigration Department that only those should be invited and admitted to this country who can be properly assimilated.
I wish to take one further general subject under review before I sit down, and it is a very important one. I refer to the frightful increase of the pernicious drug habit on the Pacific coast. This evil is not by any means restricted to British Columbia, but is gradually spreading to eastern cities, and while not wholly attributable to the Asiatic, yet the basis of the traffic is Asiatic. We have seen in Victoria and Vancouver and in other cities, but in these two in particular, almost innumerable cases of clean, decent, respectable young women from some of the best homes dragged down by the dope traffic, and very, very largely through the medium of the opium dens in the Chinese quarters. I am going to bring to the attention of the committee a little evidence that came to my hands this morning, and I have literally reams of it if 1 chose to burden the committee with it. This evidence came to me in this morning's mail in the shape of clippings from the Vancouver Sun and other Vancouver papers, showing the situation out there. Let me read very briefly a few extracts. The first is an extract from the Vancouver Sun, and refers to the provincial jail just outside of Vancouver:
Of the 320 inmates of Oakalla prison, at the present time 110 are drug addicts. This an-

nouncement was made at last nights mass meeting by Dr. Hoyes, prison doctor.
I think that authority is sufficient. This was at a mass meeting called by the United Veterans at which the business men of the city, the Board of Trade, Kiwanians, Rotar-ians, and the various other organizations common to a Canadian city, together with the war veterans and others, were present. The report goes on:
As a result of a meeting held last night in the City Hall council chamber, it was decided to call at once on the Dominion Government to bring in drastic amendments to the Drug Act that will provide severe penalties for drug traffickers.
Let me just say here that the trafficker in drugs corresponds to the bootlegger in the liquor traffic, but he is infinitely more evil in his purposes and practices than the commonest of bootleggers. The quantity of drugs it is necessary to carry is so small, and so very valuable, that detection is very difficult, and every conceivable device is resorted to in order to secure the admission of the drug and to distribute it. A man could very easily handle in a very small space thousands of dollars worth of opium or cocaine, and that is commonly done.
The report goes on:
A committee composed of civic officials and members of public organizations was formed to draft the amendments, which will be brought before another meeting to be held next Wednesday, and when they have been passed will be forwarded to Ottawa with the demand that urgent action be taken.
I read that just to indicate the nature of this meeting. Chief of Police Anderson of Vancouver had this to say:
The drug evil is a very insidious thing and not confined to any part of the community or country, but is an international question. It is no new thing to the police. We have battled with it for years and have never relaxed in our efforts.
The report goes on to say a great deal of the evils of the traffic, with which I shall not burden the committee. What I wish to bring to the attention of the minister in particular, and of the committee is this: I would urge as forcibly as I can that any Oriental found guilty of trafficking in drugs should be deported at once. There is nothing the Oriental fears more than deportation. He does not want to be deported because Canada is a veritable paradise to him as far as money making is concerned, and he does not desire to go back to China. Such a step would have a deterrent effect. I also urge strongly-and if the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty)

were here I would address these remarks to him-that those of the white race, citizens of this country, found trafficking in drugs should be punished with more severity than the law at present provides. We should also take up the great question of dealing with the poor victims of the traffic, but that is another matter not strictly connected with immigraion. My intention in bringing this subject to the notice of the committee at this time is to see to it that the basis of this traffic, the Oriental living in the country, is given to understand that the life of Canada is not going to be prostituted for the sake of providing some gain for those who carry on this traffic. Just to show that even the Orientals themselves recognize the seriousness of this business, I may say that I have in my hand the report of an organization formed only a week or so ago in Vancouver, headed by the Chinese consul, which recognizes the danger that faces these people themselves in inviting public indignation, and which has taken steps to deal with the traffic to a certain extent. But it is the duty of this Parliament, and particularly of the Administration, to deal in the most severe manner with any Oriental found indulging in or trafficking with drugs in this country. I do not wish to delay the committee at greater length. This problem is an intensely important one, and I have given but a few points in connection with it; but its significance is such that I cannot over-estimate or over-emphasize it. Canada wants, as I said at the outset, bona fide settlers; we want pioneers, but not parasites. We want men who will go and settle the country, but we do not want a race of persons coming into Canada who, experience shows beyond all question, are incapable of assimilation, and who will not take part in building up the country from its raw state.

I listened this afternoon with a great deal of care and attention to the speech of the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder), and I think I may fairly summarize it as amounting to a request for counsel and advice. The minister gave the committee a complete demonstration of the work of his department, and he seemed to be so anxious to obtain advice that he forgot, as the member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), observed to announce the policy of the Government. However, upon that observation of my hon. friend the minister submitted the Government's policy, and I must say that, to a

large extent, I am quite pleased and satisfied with that policy, my only objection being that it does not go far enough. According to the minister, there are at present hundreds of thousands of people in Europe who are only awaiting an opportunity to come and settle in Canada. Well, if I were the minister I would give them a chance to do so. I would do nothing indiscriminate or indiscreet, but I would make my gauge as wide as possible and allow them to come into the country on as large a scale as conditions would permit.
