My policy would be to make sure of the physical and moral fitness of all applicants, and if I were satisfied that in those respects they wholly complied with the standards I would set, I would admit them, provided they were not of such an age that they would become a liability rather than an asset to the country. I believe that every man, woman and child in Europe whom we can possibly accommodate, whose physical condition is satisfactory, and whose morals are such as would ensure their becoming good Canadian citizens, should be admitted into this country. There might be reservations as to the amount of money which immigrants should have, but I would not insist upon that requirement, because, after all, it is not the amount of money which a man has in his pocket when he comes to this country that will make him either an asset or a liability; it is his own personality, his own self, if I may say so. We require that every male immigrant shall have $250. Well, that is only two months' wages of the average workman in this country. All through last winter shanty men had been working and earning salaries ranging from $100 to $175 per month. Now, it might very well happen that an immigrant, who might possibly prove a wonderful asset to the country, would not be able to show $250, because we can quite understand under what conditions these people exist in Europe to-day. Europe is filled with millions of people who lost their all in the war, and I do not see how the Government can reasonably ask a man, who might be of great value to the country, to work over there and save $250 in order to come here. We know that it is a physical impossibility for a great many of them to do this. In years past it was said that a good immigrant coming into this country was worth a thousand dollars to the state. If an immigrant who will make a first-class citizen is such an asset to the country, why should we not admit every good immigrant who can come?
One of the objections raised is the question of unemployment; it is asked: how are we going to accomodate hundreds of thousands of people when there are already thousands out of employment? My answer is that unemployment does not depend upon population; it is due to temporary economic conditions. For instance, if in the United States to-day, with a population of 110,000,000, 'they have not proportionately greater unemployment than we have in Canada, that is a good argument against the theory that unemployment is attributable to largeness of population. In this country we have great natural resources, vast areas and everything to take care of millions of immigrants, and in my opinion, unemployment is very often due to the fact that men will not do the work that waits to be done. When there are between half a million and a million people in this country without homes, and Mister Bricklayer is to-day asking $1.25 an hour for laying bricks let him cut down his price and there will be employment. Let the man who would not work in the shanties for less than $100, or $125, or $150 per month cut down his price; lumber will then be cheaper and there will be employment. The conditions created by the war are abnormal. Labour has come to think that it must get its price or it will not work. Well, my policy for solving the difficulty is this: let us get the people from Europe to come to Canada and work at reasonable wages if the people of this country will not do so. Let us get these people to build our railways, and develop our forests, our agricultural resources and our other natural resources; let them come to this country and take part in its general development and let them produce. It is not so very long ago since the Minister of Trade and Commerce, speaking of the ways by which Canada would be enabled to pay its enormous debt, was making this appeal: Strive, work, produce. That is what he was saying and that is what any sane man in this country would say. We have to work and produce, and if every unemployed person in Canada would work at a reasonable rate there would be employment for every one.
Let us look through the country to-day. Let us go west or let us go east, and we will find that the farmer is seeking everywhere for labour. On the other hand the cities are crowded with hundreds of thousands of people who have left the farm because farming was not good enough for them. These people prefer leaving behind their "goodly acres", to use the poet's ex-

or three European ports, and thus save the rejected from the hardships to which they are exposed when they are sent back from this side. We must never forget that a great many of these intending immigrants are practically starving, and how can they undertake to pay their passage to Canada if they are not sure of being accepted when they come here? When they are returned to Europe they are in a far worse condition than when they left for our ports.

I am glad to hear that.
But it seems to me it would be worth while to have two or three officials in Europe to examine these people, especially if the Government is to adopt the policy of opening wider our doors to European immigration, because if I understood the minister rightly this afternoon, the Government seems open to conviction on this point. Therefore, I want to place myself on record as being in favour of admitting as many immigrants as we can get, so long, as I have already said several times, they are physically, morally and mentally fit to come here.
Now, as to subsidizing farmers, I am afraid we cannot afford to go into that venture at the present time. We have been doing this for the soldiers, but they had peculiar claims to the attention and care of the Government. For the present I would not go to that extent, but it is a proposition which might be considered a little later. The minister said this afternoon that we are free to receive hundreds of thousands of immigrants if we are willing to receive them. I would say, then, let us make a good selection of these immigrants, but let us not be too strict; let us leave outside none who are fit physically and mentally. We must not deny admission to these people simply because we have unemployment or because some labour organization complains that the newcomers would take their jobs. We shall never develop our country through a narrow policy of that kind. What this Government must do in order to keep pace with the other nations in the unprecedented race for progress and success and development which has followed in the wake of the war; what we must do in order to bring about the quick development which we need, is to admit into our country hundreds of thousands of good immigrants.
IMr. Denis. I
Mr. Chairman-

Order.
Item stands.
Canals-Chambly: improvements, $26,000.

This amount is required for renewing the river face of upper wing dam, $20,000, and for spare lock gates, $6,000. The upper wing dam which separates the canal from the river to form the upper entrance is an old -

wooden crib structure built over eighty years ago. In spite of periodic repairs it is now in a badly decayed condition and is on the verge of collapse. It is proposed to replace the river face of the dam by a concrete wall. The amount asked for is to provide also three pairs of lock gates as spare for locks number 3, 4 and 6. The locks on the Chambly canal are of different dimensions so that gates are" not interchangeable, and spare gates for these locks are required as an assurance against prolonged interruption of navigation.
Was any money spent last year on this work.

No.
Mr. MeKENZIE:	Is the traffic on
these canals anything worth while, and of what does it chiefly consist?
The Chambly canal is part of the canal system between the Hudson river and the St. Lawrence; it connects through to New York. The traffic consists largely of coal coming up and lumber going down.

The minister says
that no money was spent last year. In volume 3 of the Auditor General's Report, page w-2, I find that $1,000 was spent.
Of course, we have on all the canals a repair staff which carries on ordinary small repairs from time to time. This appropriation is for work outside the ordinary repairs.

Item agreed to.
Canals-Carillon and Grenville:	improvements, $25,000.

The main dam at
Carillon was built in 1897. It consists of a stone-filled timber crib, the apron of which has periodically caused trouble. Repairs are necessary to the extent of the amount mentioned in order to save the main structure from complete failure.
What kind of material is used in making these repairs?
The structure consists of stone-filled timber crib.

Will tenders be called
for this work?
It is done by a repair gang along the canal.

This is in the constituency which I represent. I have often heard advocated in this House
large repairs that were not, to my mind or to any one else's mind, really necessary, but these repairs in the county of Argenteuil are necessary. Quite a number of repairs are required on this canal.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Lachine canal: improvements, $50,000.

This amount is required to repair the old bridges over lock No. 5 at Lachine. These bridges form part of the route known as the Lower Lachine road which is a main thoroughfare into the city of Montreal. The two present structures were built in 1878 and 1888 respectively and are inadequate for the present traffic, being only 16 feet wide. Pedestrians have been forced off the bridge into the canal by passing motor trucks. About 2,000 trucks and 12,000 pedestrians pass over these bridges each day during the coming season. During the fiscal year 1920, up to the date of the memorandum furnished by the department, the amount of $68,557.97 was paid to Messrs. Quinlan and Robertson, contractors, from Lachine income.

Were the pedestrians
fished out?
Yes. The hon. member knows these bridges better than I do, and he knows that the work is very urgently required.

I
thought the minister said something about an income. Is this a toll bridge?

This amount was
expended last year from income account.
How is it that the Government has to build bridges for pedestrians?
The Government must build bridges across their canals. This is part of the regular roadway.
Why does the city not build them?

Where the Government construct a canal, that is, dredge the earth out and make a canal, they must provide a bridge as part of the highway. When the Lachine canal was constructed, it was cut right through the solid earth and, therefore, the Government must provide bridges to take the places of the roadways that were there before.
The population is so dense on the two banks of the canal that

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: really two bridges are not sufficient for the movement of pedestrians and carriages. I know the city of Montreal has been for a while receiving deputations from the citizens of that district. Does the minister state that only two bridges are to be built there?

At the present time, that is all in connection with which we have work going on. I agree with the hon. member. These bridges were constructed in 1878 and 1888, and the population has increased very much since then.
To-day this is one of the most thickly populated districts. It is a manufacturing district on both banks, and really I do not know that two bridges will be a great relief to the people.
Will this amount cover the whole expenditure?
Yes.
I am conversant with conditions, and I thoroughly approve the expenditure.
Yes, it is very important.
It is absolutely necessary.

Item agreed to.
Soulanges canal: improvements, $9,500.

This is for reinforcing weir at lock No. 4, $4,500, and garage for a canal motor truck, $5,000, total $9,500. Most of the structures on the St. Lawrence canal are founded upon clay. In 1918, a serious washout occurred under the breastwork of lock No. 4, which caused an interruption to navigation for eleven days during a busy season and involved a very considerable expenditure for repairs. To guard against a recurrence of the trouble at the adjacent waste weir, it is proposed to reinforce it by steel structures. The Soulanges canal is really one of the most important canals on the St. Lawrence system.

Where is lock No. 4
situated?
I have been through the canal many times, and it is down towards the lower end that the break occurred, probably near Cedar Rapids.
I notice last year $30,000 was, voted for the same purpose. Was the full amount spent last year on those improvements?
We spent $14,941.36 out of the appropriation of last year.
I understand that this was due to a landslide.
In building the Soulanges canal, heavy banks were constructed and the clay slid out and made a very serious washout there.
This canal was built only a few years ago at a cost of fourteen or fifteen million dollars, was it not? Could the contractors not be held responsible?
Not now.
Are they dead or insolvent?

You could hardly blame the contractors because, in all these contracts for construction work, the Government have their engineers in charge right on the ground, and the contractors carry out the work under the supervision and instruction of the engineers, so that really our engineers would be to blame for an error, if there was an error.
We shall have to let it slide.

My
hon. friend said that $30,000 was voted last year and that some $14,000 of that amount was spent. In the Auditor General's Report, volume 3 page W-2, I find: "Soulanges canal improvements, $70,980.21." Where did the minister get that money?

That was to repair
the damage that occurred on account of the landslide, and a Governor General's warrant had to be issued to pay for it.
How was the money obtained? I understood the minister to say that he got a vote of $30,000 for that purpose and that he spent less than half of it. The matter requires some explanation.

The $30,000 was the ordinary vote for repairs on the canal, and $14,000 was spent on that. But we had this accident, a landslide, and $70,000 had to be expended to repair the canal. In a case of that kind, where an accident happens, the only way in which you can get the money to' pay for the necessary work is by a Governor General's warrant. That item will appear in the list of Governor General's warrants.

Does
not this money have to be voted afterwards?
Yes, but it was paid by Governor General's warrant.

Does
Parliament get no notice of these payments by Governor General's warrant.
Yes, ten days after Parliament meets a list of all the Governor General's warrants is laid on the table.

Although what I am
going to refer to probably does not come under this item, may I ask whether it is the intention to light the Rideau canal this year?

I could not say. That
comes under the Marine Department. This item of $25,000 is to provide a new tug. The destruction by fire of the old Soulanges gasoline launch last summer leaves the Soulanges canal without any tug boat, thereby greatly increasing material transportation costs. On the other hand, the Quebec canal dredging fleet has two tugs, the Frank Perew, an old tug built over 50 years ago and practically falling to pieces, and burning a ton of coal per hour, and the Carillon which has no berth accommodation for the crew and must always be accompanied by the Ark.

Where is this new tug
going to be built?

We shall call for
tenders if we decide to get a new tug. I have been seeing if we could not get a second-hand tug at a very much less cost. We had an offer of a steel tug at $20,000, but I thought that was too high. We may possibly be able to get a second-hand tug for less than this amount. In case we buy a new tug, tenders will be called for and the contract awarded to the lowest tenderer.

Has
the minister a whole fleet of these tug's? I see that this item is for the Quebec dredging fleet. I have heard of the navy and of the merchant marine, but I never heard of the Quebec dredging fleet before.
It is a fleet of small dredges working along the canals to keep them clear.
What does the coal cost on these tugs?
It depends where it comes from. Nova Scotia coal is pretty high.

It is $8 a ton. I
suppose the tug that my hon. friend said burned a ton of coal an hour works ten hours a day, and that therefore she would consume about $80 worth of coal a day.
We have abandoned her.
How long was she carrying on with that capacity for burning coal?
Could we not turn that obsolete tug over to the Department of Marine to be used in connection with the Canadian Navy?	,
Would the minister say who made the offer of a second-hand tug in Montreal?

We advertised in the newspapers and there were about a dozen replies. The nearest to what we wanted came from a man in Montreal. I cannot remember his name just now, but he had a steel tug. We thought the price he wanted was too high, and we have not done anything about it.
Was that tug on the Cornwall canal?
I think it was at Sorel.
Did this offer of a tug come from the Sorel Shipbuilding and Dry Dock Company, from Mr. S. McNaugh-ton, or the Leclair Shipbuilding Company?
Or from L. Cohen and Sons?
I do not remember.
Did I understand the minister to say that the tug Frank Perew was destroyed?
We are abandoning her. She is 50 years old.
Is the minister keeping her crew on? '
We are not keeping any crew until we can get a tug. This boat was abandoned last fall. We have not stai'ted work on the canals yet this season.
Would the minister tell us at what price he was offered the secondhand tug in Montreal?
For $20,000. It was a second-hand tug, 8 or 10 years old, and required a lot of repairs. I thought it would be better to buy a new tug, and for that reason we did not accept the offer.
What would a brand-' new tug cost?

Twenty-five thousand
dollars is the estimate given to me.
How much does it cost the Government to keep that Quebec dredging fleet at work the whole season?
$9,083.78, as shoTfrn on page W-3 of the Auditor General's report.
On page W-92 of the Auditor General's report under the heading of "Quebec Canals" I find the amount stated at $31,349.47.

If my hon. friend wfll turn to the next page, W-93, he will find that the dredge vessels of the Quebec Canals cost $9,083.75. In the $32,000 odd there is included the "Lachine canal, income, dredging," $16,652.77, and the bonus votes.
St. Anne's lock: improvements, $3,500.
This amount is required for renewing the upper entrance to the pier. It will complete the work of renewing the top of the timber crib with concrete. This is one of our most important locks.
Where is it?
As you come in from the St. Lawrence up the Ottawa, the St. Anne's lock is below the Grand Trunk bridge.

Item agreed to.
St. Ours lock: improvements, $4,500.

This is required to
renew the tops of two mooring piers above the St. Ours lock in the Richelieu river. The piers are required as anchors during the placing and removing of flash boards on the dam, and also during repairs to the dam. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Trent: Improvements, $515,000.

This sum is to be
expended on the following work: New lock and dam at Bobcaygeon, $205,000; at Lake-field, $40,000; Otonabee river dams, Nassau, $175,000; construction of lock guage, $25,000; reservoir dams, $25,500; Mississauga lake dams, $8,000; concrete railings for river walls, $6,000; painting lift locks, $6,000; miscellaneous works, $9,500. This
fMr J. D. Reid.]
is a part of the Trent canal system and the new lock at Bobcaygeon, for which $205,000 is required, has been delayed so long that it is now imperative that the work should be proceeded with.
Why?

The locks have got
into a serious condition.
Do you say that the lock at present is not in proper condition and could not stand for another season?
No, we kept it going during the war, but the engineers have at last reported that they will no longer take the responsibility if anything happens.
Have you the report of the engineer?
No.
I should like to see it.

The engineers have
reported that the Bobcaygeon lock, the Nassau dam and the Lakefield dam are in imperative need of repair, and that the city of Peterborough and other places are in grave danger if the work is not proceeded with. It has ben already too long deferred.
What is the character of the damage already done?

There has been none
so far.

These structures were in
good condition until the close of last season, were they not?

No; for some time
past their condition has been dangerous.

Are these the amounts
that are to cover contracts awarded just prior to the Peterborough election? I understood from the press reports at the time that large contracts were awarded a week prior to the taking of the vote in Peterborough.
No. The hon. member surely does not think we would do a thing of that kind.
Oh, no.

Honi soit qui mal y
pense.
The Bobcayegon contract must have been let a year and a half ago.

Has any work bees
done there?

Yes, it must be half
through.

How much money was
spent there last year?

The date of the
contract is December 12, 1919, which was a long time before the Peterborough election. The sum of $122,000 has been spent on that contract.

What will be the
total?
caygeon lock?

been spent, leaving a
Is is estimated at
That is, the Bob-
Yes; $122,000 has balance of $204,000.
When was the contract awarded for the dam on the Otonabee river for $175,000? Was not that awarded a week prior to the Peterborough election?

It was awarded on
the 4th February, 1921.

I struck the right
number that time.
So that it was three days before the election.
That vote had been made a long time before, and we never thought of it in connection with the election.
Before this item is voted-
It will not be voted.

The committee is entitled to further information regarding the report of the engineers. The minister says that a report was made in due form, specifying certain repairs. The committee should have that report for perusal. There seems to be a suspicion on this side that these repairs were ordered and the contracts awarded when a certain election was impending, and it seems strange that the minister should not be able to put his hand upon the report now. These expenditures are pretty large, and I see also that repairs are being made on the canal near the Chateau Laurier. I do not see anything quoted last year for these repairs, and I want some information in regard to this matter.

These items for Bobcay-geon and Lakefield were voted a year ago,
and the contracts let in 1919. At that time I had the report of the engineers. The Nassau dam has been in the Estimates too, for, I think, about three years.
But it had to be revoted.

Yes, I know. This dam is owned by the Canadian General Electric Company, whose power house is connected therewith, and the department is under obligation to maintain the dam in perpetuity. An appropriation was voted last session to proceed with reconstruction of the dam.
What was the amount last year?
Fifty thousand dollars, I think; there has been a certain amount every year.
That was voted; how much was spent last year?

There was nothing spent on it. We had to make an arrangement with the Canadian General Electric that they should pay a share of the cost of completing the renewal of the dam. But this was at the time we took over the Trent canal and we had to agree that the dam would be maintained there in perpetuity.
When did you take over the Trent canal?
Oh, that was at Confederation; at least many years ago.

Is the proposed work an
extension of the existing system?

No, it is one of the
old dams that was on the Trent canal. There are a number of water powers and dams that have been there for very many years.

Are you renewing them
entirely?

This is one we have
to renew entirely because if there was a break it would be a very serious matter for the town of Peterborough. The dam is above Peterborough.
I think Peterborough should look after itself. I would like to know whether this is a completely new work? Has the dam got to be repaired, or is a new dam required?

It is a completely new dam.

Mr. V1EN: Are you going to rebuild it on a very extensive scale?

The construction will
be of a more permanent character. We are putting in concrete now.
What was the nature of the first dam?

Just wood filled with
stone. We are now making the dam more permanent.

The minister a few
minutes ago informed us that the contract for rebuilding the dam on the Otonabee river, amounting to $175,000, was awarded on February 4, 1921, or just three days prior to the election in Peterborough. Does this not appear to the committee as being rather significant? I think it is only fair that the committee should have the report of the engineer justifying the expenditure of this amount of money. It is something more than a coincidence that the contract should have been awarded on the date referred to and that the election took place only three days afterwards.

Well, Mr. Chairman,
I have no objection to let the item stand, and permit any hon. member to see the whole of the file dealing with this matter from beginning to end.

Before the item
stands I wish to ask how much money was spent on the Trent canal last year. I see an item of $427,000, and there is a re-vote of $25,000. Does the total of $452,000 represent the expenditure last year?

No, In round numbers
$350,000 was spent last year. In reference to the Nassau dam I could send a copy of the engineer's report to any hon. member who wishes to see it. Or he can take the file and peruse the whole of the documents to be found there-I have no objection to letting him do so. I will send an official with the papers to any member who wishes to see the file and in the meantime we will let the item stand.

Not only in respect to the
Nassau dam, but I would like to see the papers in regard to the whole of the improvements on the Trent canal covering the expenditure made on that canal last year. I suppose the minister understands what I mean?	.

I have no objection at all. I am willing to send an official with the files to the hon. member, or if he prefers
CMr J. D. Reid.]
he can come to the department and see them.
I would prefer that the minister would send an official with the file to my room at ten o'clock to-morrow.

Well, I will send the
Chief Engineer, Mr. Bowden, over with the whole file.

I would like the minister to understand that what I want is the file showing not only the whole of the details as to the Trent canal improve-
10 p.m. ment for this year, but also all the details of the expenditure on those improvements last year.
Certainly, I understand.

Are we not to be furnished with particulars regarding the item on page 33 "Chargeable to Capital $139,000?" I do not think that has been passed. It seems to me that these two items should be taken together, and the total of the two is over $800,000.

We will come to that
item in a few minutes and we will then find out what the committee wants.
I should like some information from the minister as to the class of freight that passes through the Trent canal.

It is all local freight.
The reason for that is that part of the Trent canal is not yet completed-that is the upper entrance to the Georgian bay. There. is a little more work to be done but when that is completed freight can be caried from the Georgian bay right through to the St. Lawrence.

This canal has been in
existence for a great many years. Is the traffic heavy on it?

No, it will not be heavy until the canal is completed. There is another matter in connection with the building of the Trent canal which I think is worthy of consideration. Its construction will furnish a good waterway, and if the system is ever completed right through to the Georgian bay it will afford a cheap route for bringing grain from the Georgian bay to the St. Lawrence river.
Mr, CAMPBELL:	Does the minister
really think that?

Yes, I do and I will
tell the hon. member why. If the hon.

member knows that territory at all, he knows that it will give a very short route from the Georgian hay to the St. Lawrence river. On account of its being a small canal, about a thousand ton barge canal, I suppose the hon. member feels it would not pay to take grain through it. Well, if my memory serves me right about two-thirds of the grain that was formerly carried through, Buffalo for New York went through the Erie canal and the vessels on the Trent canal have a larger capacity than those on the Erie canal.
At present?

The Erie canal was
rebuilt I think, four or five years ago. What I say is that for the last twenty-five or thirty years the barges that carried so much grain on the old Erie canal were smaller than the barges that go through the Trent canal.

How do they compare with
the vessels on the new Erie canal?

I am informed they are thirteen, or fifteen, hundred tons as compared with a thousand tons-that is about the difference. The Trent canal will give a great tourist route through a very attractive country. There has also been a very large amount of power developed owing to the construction of that canal.

I would like to follow this
matter a little bit further in view of the fact that these sums are being voted annually. We are asked to vote a considerable sum of money each year for the Trent canal and up to the present we are getting very poor returns for it. In view of the fact that there are many places needing transportation facilities at the present time the thought occurred to me that it would be well to make this a permanent route by using this money to macadamize it, or something of the kind.

If this money is not
expended very serious damage will result to the towns along the route by reason of these locks and dams washing away.

Before the item stands I would like to have some information from the minister regarding a certain contract with the Canadian General Electric Company, to which he referred a few minutes ago. The minister said, if I understood him properly, that he was bound to keep these locks or dams in repair because he had a contract with this company. Surely if a contract exists with the company the
company ought to be made to pay its share. I think it is in better financial standing even than the Government; its credit is higher.

I said a power dam
was built there many years ago, which the Government had to build and keep in repair in perpetuity. That dam is worn out and must be repaired, otherwise the Government would be responsible for any damage that resulted if the dam were washed away. In reconstructing the dam any extra work over and above what would be the Government's regular share the Canadian General Electric will pay. We are looking after that, but as a matter of fact there never was any objection by the company to paying its share. That is the situation.
Is there a contract between the Government and the company to that effect?
Yes.

Could the minister
make a copy of that contract a part of the file which will be exhibited to the hon. member for Lotbiniere?	*
All contracts in connec-' tion with the Trent canal are on the one file.

How much of last year's
vote was expended on the Trent Canal improvements?

About $350,000 for
permanent improvements.
What is the total estimate of the proposed improvements on the Trent canal?
There is some work to be done at the upper entrance, but I have not got an estimate yet. That is for capital account.
It takes a lot.of capital.

Yes, it does. I myself always felt, probably like many other members, that we were not warranted in making that expenditure on the Trent canal, but after going through the canal two years ago I must say that I think the expenditure was warranted. It started many years ago when both parties were urging the construction of this canal.

What
was the traffic on the canal last year?

Those statistics are
kept in the Trade and Commerce Department.
Did the minister see any freight traffic on that trip?
Yes, there were several large steamers running principally from Peterborough up through lake Simcoe as far as Orillia.
Pleasure boats?

No, quite large
steamers.
Under 1,000 tons?
About 1,000 tons.

While the deputy minister
is looking up information for the member for Guysborough, I might draw the minister's attention to the fact that there is considerable water-power along this canal.
Yes.
What is the total quantity of water-power leased by the Federal Government along that line, and what is the revenue received from it?

When I went through the canal, if I remember rightly, about
125,000	horse-power was capable of development; that is, some of the locks where the dams were they were not using. The Sun Life Company owned the water-power there, and the Hydro Electric purchased it. The revenue from that was about $2 per horse-power under some leases and under others less. As the hon. member will recollect from the discussions in the House on previous occasions, some of the leases were granted at a very low rental. The Hydro Electric-I am trusting to my memory now-is paying to the Federal Government $60,000 to $70,000 a year. They took issue as to our being entitled to that revenue, claiming that it belonged to the Ontario Government. However, the courts decided the matter in our favour recently. We got a cheque from the Hydro Electric a few days ago for $125,000 on account of the rental since they took the lease over three years ago.

Are not the leases on that canal similar to the leases on all our other canals? They were originally fixed on a $2 basis, in consideration of the lessee doing a certain amount of the development work?
Yes.

The lessee pays for the
water and does the development work-the head race leading up to the flume.
Yes.
Did I understand the minister to say that if this dam was not maintained the lessee would have no water power?

Yes, the hon. member
is right. That dam was built many years ago, and we must maintain it.
Is not the dam part of the development work?
No.

You
could not develop power without the dam.

The dam was constructed at Lakefield to build the lock, and of course that dam must be maintained. When it was constructed the power was sold to certain persons in perpetuity, and we agreed to maintain the dam. There are a number of leases on all of our canals, and some (of them are for ninety-nine years, some for a longer term, and others for terms of twenty or twenty-five years. A good many of those leases have been expiring during the past few years. Some years ago the Government passed an Order in Council raising the rate of $2 up to $4, $5 and $6. I think $6 is now our limit. The rate depends on the quantity of power that is taken; for a small quantity it is $6, if a larger quantity is taken the rate is a little less.

They
built the dam for the purpose of navigation?
Yes.

Then
it was discovered that it developed power?
Yes.

And
the powers have been leased to the Hydro Electric?
Yes.

At a
very low rate.

And the Canadian General
Electric.

Or
some company. It strikes me that the repairs ought to be done by that company. That is part of the work of keeping up

the system, and it seems to me rather unreasonable that if the Government is selling the power at such a very low rate it should have to keep that dam in repair. According to the minister we are building a new dam. Does he intend to develop power there?

We are only renewing an old dam, we are not building a new dam at another point. This old dam has been in existence for a great many years. As the hon. member states, some of this power is leased to the Hydro Electric and some to the Canadian General Electric. It was leased many years ago, not by this Government. Probably the leases held by [DOT] the Canadian General Electric and the Hydro Electric were granted many years ago by the Dominion Government to the original lessees. The Hydro Electric simply got a transfer of the Seymour Power Company's interests. That company got some old leases from lessees that had been granted them probably thirty or forty years ago for terms running from fifty to sixty years. Then they got some other powers as they were developed along the Trent canal. I think that during the time Mr. Graham was minister the Seymour Power Company got some additional power, Mr. Graham charging them a rental which was fair and reasonable, having regard to the prices being paid for power at that time. The Hydro Electric simply takes over these leases and carries out the contract that the Seymour Power Company had, paying the same rental.
Can the minister now answer my question about the traffic?

Fifty-three thousand
tons of traffic passed through the canal last year, consisting mostly of forest, mineral and agricultural products. Some coal from across Lake Ontario, is put into these small boats and goes from Trenton up to Peterborough. In that way it has had quite an effect, or will have, of reducing freight rates through water competition. There is quite a large manufacturing district along the Trent canal. There is Campbellford, quite a manufacturing centre, Peterborough, Lakefield and on up to Orillia.
Do I understand the minister to say that the operation of this route keeps down the freight rates on the railways?
Water competition assists in cheapening rates.

The minister does
contend that it keeps down the rates on the railways?
Yes.
We have the information to-day that our railroads are in need of traffic. What is the use of creating another highway to take traffic from railways which are already short of traffic?

This is not a new project. I was in this House thirty-one years ago, and they had started it then. It is simply a matter of repairing work that was done many years ago, and the repairs are quite necessary. The amount spent on this waterway system up to the present time is $18,000,000. We have 125,000 horse-power developed and we have a waterway which I believe will be of great advantage after it gets through to the Georgian Bay canal.
Mr. REID (Mackenzie)): Even if this work had been started in the days of Adam, that would not mean that we would have to continue it if it was of no benefit. Strange to say, the amounts for this canal do not all appear- on the same page of the Estimates, and that is rather confusing. We find that the total asked for this year is $864,000. How many feet of water is on top of the sills of the locks in this canal?
From Peterborough up, eight feet, and six feet between Peterborough and Lake Ontario. It will accommodate a 1000-ton barge.

According to the minister, the traffic which passed through this canal last year was a mere bagatelle, only five or six ordinary shiploads. It appears that we are developing hydro-electric power there but we are not aiding navigation at all; it is not a commercial venture so far as navigation is concerned. I always had an idea that this canal was started as an election canal; it generally crops up when there is an election contest in that vicinity. If it has been going on in this way for thirty years and we have been spending three or four hundred thousand dollars year on it, is it not time to call a halt, when money is so scarce? We should not be spending large sums on such a venture at a time like this. I suppose the province of Ontario makes money out of the power which is developed there, but that does not help the commerce

of the country or justify the existence of the canal for commercial purposes. I notice by the report of the Auditor General, volume 3, page W-3, that my hon. friend has a staff of officers on the canal which cost the country last year $97,218.42. That is a very large amount to pay for the business done on that canal. I would like to have a list of these officers.

The details will be
found on page W-107 of the Auditor Gen-ehal's report, volume 3.
Are all these officers necessary?
Yes, at every lock you have to have a lockmaster and one or two men.

According to the
figures given in the Auditor General's report, there is an expenditure on staff alone of almost $2 a ton for the amount of traffic handled, and I assume that other incidental expenses must be added to that. It is a very large amount of money to spend for that amount of traffic.
The minister has said that 125,000 horse-power is developed along this canal at a value of $2 per horsepower, or $250,000.
I said that the whole of the 125,000 had not been used.
How much did the department receive last year from that source, how much from freight traffic, and what was the entire revenue derived last year from the operation of the canal?

No tolls are charged on the canals; there is no revenue from that source. I will give the hon. member the information as regards the revenue for the water-power. The Hydro Electric took issue with us after they got the Seymour Power Company; they claimed that that power belonged to the Ontario Government and that the rental should, therefore, go to the Ontario Government. It was a case of a private owner claiming that he should not pay for power. The case was tried with the result, of course, that the Ontario Government won its case. The Hydro Electric have admitted that they should pay this, and they have paid $125,000 on account.
For arrears?

Yes. There is so
much revenue that we should get from
[Mr. Sinclair.1
the power users. That has all been collected, save a balance that is yet due by the Hydro Electric who have agreed to pay it and we expect it almost every day.

The information which '
the minister is to give would cover actual contracts in force at the present time.
Yes.

If, as the minister
states,-and I have no doubt that what he states is correct,-the Ontario Government and the Hydro Electric are disputing the right of the federal Government to control this canal, I would suggest-
They do not do so now, as regards the Trent canal. That matter has been settled.

That is rather unfortunate, because, in view of the results obtained in the operation of that canal, it would be entirely in the interests of the federal Government if the Ontario Government were made a present of this canal and made to look after these repairs and so on. I do not think the federal Government have anything to gain by holding this canal. It would be a sound proposition if they would induce the Hydro Electric and the Ontario Government to take the thing over altogether.

The Ontario Government are not anxious to take this over. They seem to be operating the Timis-kaming road successfully, and I would not mind giving them the National Transcontinental too if they would take it.

I am not disposed to agree with the minister and the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) as regards handing this over to the province of Ontario or the Hydro Electric Commission. If, as the minister says, there is
125,000	horse-power available now, with the possibility of greater development, at the minimum price of $2 established years ago for this water-power, it is worth at least $250,000 a year in revenue.
Easily that.

With the rearrangement
proposed by the department a few years ago of the rentals on all the canals, and with the increased cost and value of power, this will be a rather valuable asset to the Dominion. I do not see why, if there is a readjustment of these rentals, there should not be an even greater revenue to

the Dominion. I can understand that it would be hard to raise the rentals on some of the old leases that are made for ninety-nine years, but on the new leases there should be an increase on the present price of $2.

I agree with the hon.
member, and I was agreeably surprised when I went through to find that we had developed 125,000 horse-power and built all those locks and made a good canal at a cost of $18,000,000 odd, or possibly less than $150 a horse-power. I also feel, having gone through that canal, that if we ever get it through to Georgian hay- and there is very little work to be done now-this will he quite a route for bringing grain down from Georgian bay points. It is a short route and these water routes help to cheapen transportation.

The hon. member for
Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) takes issue with my suggestion. The situation seems to me to be like this. The minister has told us that he has been in the House for thirty-one years and that during all that time the experience obtained by him and the federal Government has been very little different from what it seems to be now. The situation seems to be: "Live horse and you will get grass." You will get revenue in years to come. If we go on spending money year after year in this way, I cannot see any good business sense behind this proposition. In 1919-20 if you look at the Auditor General's Report, Volume III, page W-2, you will find this amount spent for Trent canal improvements, $77,251.36. On page W-3 there are these further items:	Trent canal staff,
$97, 218.42; Trent canal repairs, $63,343.48, or somewhere in the neighbourhood of $200,000 spent on the Trent canal in 191920. We have a further demand in this item for Trent canal improvements of $515,000 and the item to rebuild wharf at Lindsay, $10,000. I think the minister stated that the revenue was in the neighbourhood of about fifty or sixty thousand dollars. If the minister calls that good business, I take issue with him, and I would object to the federal Government continuing to own this property. It would be good business if the federal Government could get rid of this along with the National Transcontinental and several other things, if they could hand these things over to the Provincial Government of Ontario who seem to be making a success of these things. Bv the way, they are making the
Temiskarning and Northern Ontario a paying proposition. If they can make the Trent canal a paying proposition and the Canadian National Railways a paying proposition, the federal Government should hand over these federal white elephants to the Ontario Government, as they _ seem to be able to make a success of similar propositions.

The minister, a few
minutes ago, made a statement which we are all aware of, but which I have never been able to understand, and it is that the canals of Canada are free, The Dominion of Canada has hundreds of millions of dollars of capital invested in the canals of this country. I for one fail to understand why those canals should not be made at least self-sustaining. Why does public property in the shape of canals not receive an adequate return to sustain it, whereas in the case of other transportation systems, such as railways, the Government makes a charge? The public canals are used by private interests for their benefit, and I do not see why they should not pay for what they get. I may be desperately ignorant on something that is generally accepted as a proper procedure.

About 1897 or 1898
when the Hon. Mr. Blair was minister, the canals were made free for this reason: The Americans took off the tolls on the American canals, and if we had kept the tolls on the Welland and St. Lawrence canals, of course, all traffic from the West would go via Buffalo to New York. The canal tolls on a cargo of grain amount to a few hundred dollars, and a small fraction will turn the grain by another route. We wanted this grain, produced in Canada, to be transported via our own canals.

It is going to the
United States just the same.

It was the Welland
canal and the St. Lawrence canals that they had mostly in mind when they made all the canals free.

Are
the American canals still free?

Yes, they are all
free.

Does the minister think
the country is compensated in any way for the heavy expenditure it has made on these canals by making them free?

I can remember when
we collected in tolls on the canals about $500,000 a year. Now if you collect that much, it means just that much off the value of the goods through the canals. The enlargement of the Welland canal and the St. Lawrence canals very materially reduced the rate. I can remember when vessels 'passed through those canals with a cargo of 20,000 bushels, and the rates were very high. Then the Government of the day decided to enlarge the Welland canal and the St. Lawrence canals to accommodate vessels of 14 feet draft and 253 feet in length. The late John Page, who was chief engineer at that time, when constructing the canals said that they would be good for 50 or 100 years.
When was that?

That is probably 30
years ago, but the enlargement to 14 feet had hardly been completed when the canals were again found too small for larger vessels, with larger cargoes. I can remember when we paid 20 cents a bushel on grain from Chicago to Prescott, at the head of the St. Lawrence canals, and I can remember that just prior to the war the rate on grain from Port Arthur to Prescott was as low as 2 cents a bushel. If times were normal, and wages were as they were before the war, my opinion is that grain could be brought from Port Arthur and Fort William to Prescott or Kingston for about 3 cents a bushel, and one-and-a-half cents from Kingston to Montreal.
Via the Trent canal?

No, via the Welland
and St. Lawrence canals. My hon. friend from Huntingdon knows this canal system practically as well as I do, if not better, and I think he can corroborate my statement that the Beauharnois canal, when it was enlarged to 14 feet, was found too small even then.

I am not finding fault with the work of enlarging these canals and reducing the transportatidn .costs. I am very glad indeed if the cost of transporting grain from the west has been reduced, as the minister states, from 20 to 2 cents a bushel, but I think that is all the more reason why those who are transporting the grain can afford to pay something for the privilege of using the canals constructed by the money of the people of all Canada. My point is this: if it is right to use public money for the purpose of making transportation free for the benefit of 	.
private individuals, why not make the railways free too? I am not advocating that you should, but I do believe that the principle is right that the users of the public canals of Canada should pay the cost of maintaining the canals.

If we had a toll on grain coming from the West via the St. Lawrence route, it would mean one of two things; either that the farmers of the West must take less for their grain, or else it would go via the Erie canal and New York, where there are no tolls.

It goes that way
now, does it not?
It goes via the St. Lawrence.
The bulk of it goes via Buffalo.
During the last two or three years perhaps, but prior to the war the bulk of it went down the St. Lawrence.
And since the war?

It is coming back
again. We cannot get the grain to come via the St. Lawrence route if we put the tolls on, unless the farmer will take less for his grain.

Why not take the grain over the Transcontinental from Winnipeg to Quebec? The distance is much shorter than over any other railway. That system of transportation has never been taken full advantage of by the present Administration or its predecessor. There is some mystery about it that can only be explained when the minister condescends to take the House into his confidence.
That will come up when we are discussing the railways.

We will surely not forget the minister on that occasion. In connection with this item, there is something that is absolutely unjustifiable. We are asked to pay $97,000 in wages alone to employees of a canal which carried 53,000 tons of freight in a year. That item of $97,000 is for wages alone; it does not cover maintenance or other expenses. Last year we were asked to vote for Trent canal improvements $427,000, of which amount the minister says $350,000 was expended. This year we are called upon to vote an item of $515,000 for the same canal. I say that that is absolutely unjustifiable, and I do

not think the House will believe the minister when he says that this is only for maintenance and absolutely urgent repairs.
And there is another $10,000.

Yes, and $10,000 to rebuild a wharf at Lindsay last year, and $9,000 this year, and there are other items at different places in the Estimates. I say that this looks much more like general elections than General Electric. I think that this item should stand until full particulars have been given by the minister.
It was to stand.

Yes, but we know the gentleman was once called the foxy minister, and before the hon. gentleman gets away with this item, we want to tell him the particulars in regard to which we require an explanation. He was kind enough to offer to have an official of his department here to-morrow, but we want to tell him now the particulars we want explained. One of them is the expenditure last year of $350,000, and another is the detailed information in regard to that item of $515,000 for this year. He might give us also a statement of the general scope of the improvements for which we are voting large sums of money every year. The minister says that we have already spent $18,000,000 on the Trent canal to. provide transportation facilities for 53,000 tons of freight, and I believe that this freight could easily be transported by other means of transportation in this country which have been provided at very great expense. For these reasons I should like to have a statement of the general scope of the improvements which are contemplated by the department, so that we might be able to judge as to what commitments we are faced with and what is to be done with these various votes which the department is asking the House to grant every year.

I think the minister said a few minutes ago that a contract was entered into to rebuild a part of the Trent canal, and that the contract was awarded some time previous to the Peterborough election. Was there just one tenderer, or were there more? If so, how many were there, and what was tendered by each of them?
The chief engineer tells me that there were four or five tenders. I forget myself how many there were.
Who received the contract?
R. Sheehy and Sons, Peterborough, the lowest tenderers.
Are they Conservatives?
I really do not know.
They are, surely.
I never knew the name before; I never heard of them until after the contract was given.

What is the cost of
operating and maintaining these free canals of Canada?
What canals?
All of them.

On page W-3 of the
Auditor General's report, there is given a list of the canals, and the total is $1,579,114.74. In addition to that, there is an expenditure in connection with statistical officers.

How much does that cost?
, Hon. Mr. REID:	It costs $36,360.27.

Is there any revenue
from these canals?

There is the revenue
from the water-powers. There are water-powers on all the canals- on the Welland canal there is a lot of power, and there is also power on the Soulanges, the St. Lawrence, the Lachine, and the Trent. I cannot say how much revenue is derived from these water powers.
Is all of it harnessed?

The water-power on
the Trent canal is not all harnessed; I think about 60,000 horse power has been developed, but there is potentialy about
125,000	horse power.

I understood the Hydro
Electric was short of power?

Yes, but this is in
another locality. There is plenty of power in this particular locality, some of which is privately owned.

What is the quantity
of water power produced on the Lachine canal, and through whom is it sold?

I shall have to get
that information from the office, although it is in the Auditor General's report. There are quite a large number of lessees on the Lachine canal. A good many of the leases were given seven or eight years ago, and as they expire new rates ate being charged.

There is a regular rate now. Some leases have many years to run yet at a very small rental.

Has any development
been made by the Government?

When the.canals were constructed the weirs were put in and the owners of the mills developed from them into their own factories. In building a dam it is easy to put in weirs so that the water can run through into a man's mill, and it can be done with little expense.
What is the rate charged for water-power?

It is between $4 and
$6, depending on circumstances. I shall have that information when we are on these items again. I will bring a copy of the Order in Council that fixed these rates.
Will this item complete the improvements on the Trent canal?

No. For a number of
years repairs will have to be made on the Trent canal. It was taken over at the time of Confederation and the works must be renewed. Money will have to be spent also to open up into Georgian bay.
That can stand until financial conditions are better.

We are only doing
work now that must be done.

You do not propose
to do further construction work now?
No.

Will you bring the plans
to-morrow?

Yes, Mr. Bowden will
be over with the plans of the Trent canal.
This item stands, does it not?

Yes, I am letting this item stand.
Item stands.
Trent-To rebuild wharf at Lindsay, $10,000.
I understood it was arranged with the leader of the Opposition that we should close at eleven o'clock. However, it is not quite eleven yet.

I was keeping my eye on the clock, but there are other items relating to the Trent canal here. The next one is to provide for the rebuilding of the
[Mr J. *. Reid.]
wharf at Lindsay. I had the engineer go down there and he states that the wharf should be rebuilt. My good old friend, General Hughes, made a strong plea that I should put this item in for him. I said I would and I would like the committee to pass it, it is a re-vote.
Is there any reason why these wharves should not be built by the Public Works Department?

Yes, we build a few wharves along our own canals. This is connected with our own works and our own men build them. This wharf was built by us a good many years ago and it is in a very bad state of repair.
This is a good illustration of the policy of the Government. The minister has just stated "General Hughes asked me to put the item there and I did so."

I did not make any
such statement.

What did you say then?
Hon. Mr.. REID: I said this is a work which should have been done three or four years ago. We held off on account of the war, but the work is absolutely necessary and urgent. I also said my good friend, General Hughes, has pressed for this to he done.
That is what I said, "He has pressed for it."
It is just as urgent as any other work and I put the item in.

About two years ago there
was a tidal wave which destroyed most of the wharves along the St. Lawrence front, from about ten miles below Quebec up to Montreal, or at least to Three Rivers. In my riding of Lotbiniere there were two wharves, one of which was a government wharf at St. Croix. I urged the Government to rebuild that wharf and to give some accommodation to the population of the County because at least ten or twelve parishes used the wharf to go to the market at Quebec. The Government did not find their way clear to do so. They said the war was on, and there were so many other expenditures that had to he met. The Government indeed were too poor to spend any money in the county of Lotbiniere although the interested parties offered to give a piece of land for a deep water wharf. The Seigneur of Lotbiniere had made plans and offered to maintain the wharf if the Government

would only rebuild it. The Department of Public Works sent a special engineer down to investigate the matter. His report was favourable and the only drawback was the lack of money. A few months afterwards I received a letter from the Minister of Finance asking me to go over the county of Lotbiniere and encourage the people to subscribe as largely and generously as possible to the Victory Bonds, to the loan that the Government were then raising. I did my best, and the county subscribed $180,000 towards the management of the affairs of the country. They came to the Government and tried to induce them to spend some of that money in the riding, because many parishes thirty miles from the railroad had no other access to the market in Quebec than that afforded by the wharves at St. Croix and St. Antoine. It was of no avail-the Government (did not find their way clear to grant any money. These poor devils are still there without any wharves and without any access to the market, but the minister comes here to-night and says "General Plughes, my friend, pressed the matter so much on me that I had to put that item here. It is of course, a very urgent need for the riding of Victoria and Haliburton. The work was put off during the war but now that General Hughes is pressing so much for an item to appear in the Estimates I could not refuse that to my friend." Well, I say this is an illustration of how the money of the people of 11 p.m. Canada is spent. It is spent when friends of the Government urge it. When they press it on the ministers then the purse is opened, then the public exchequer is opened, then the public money flows freely into those ridings where it is best to let it flow, for political purposes and political aims. But I say that in circumstances like the present when the country is face to face with bankruptcy, Vhen the present administration cannot present better financial statements than the one we had from the Minister of Railways at the opening of the session, I say that it takes some-[DOT] what shall I say?-cheek, nerve, or audacity for the minister of the Crown to assert "This item was pressed on me by my good friend General Hughes". Not only this item but a great many other items have been pressed on the Government and to-day they are spending the money freely despite the dire financial
conditions that the country is faced with. They spend money freely when they see some political advantage to be derived from it. Well, I maintain that such a state of affairs should be put clearly before the public of Canada, and it seems to me that under the circumstances this item of $10,000 for a wharf at Lindsay might easily stand. Of course for the minister,-who, since the war, is used to spending millions and talking in hundreds of millions-it is a trifling amount, but $10,000 is $10,000 and if the minister would refrain from expending such sums here and there, and even larger amounts, he might find his way clear to financing his railways and canals in a more successful manner. For my part, Sir, I would be willing that the item should be struck out.
Carried.
Not carried. I move that the item be struck out.
I second the motion. I have a few words to say in reference to this item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: A motion that the item be struck out is certainly not in order. There is a motion before the committee that the item carry, but the hon. member has the fight to vote against it-
All right.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: -or to reduce the item.
That would be all right.
Carried.

Not carried. Question.
Item agreed to on division: Yeas, 31, nays 21.
